articles.title: Israel’s election commission rejects Netanyahu claims of voting fraud
articles.summary:
Move comes after attorney general blocked Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties

Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of the…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison and Quique Kierszenbaum in Jerusalem

blocks.text: Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of the 27 October vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of their governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.

His main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, warned that Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy”, attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Hours earlier Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties, because she was not presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.

“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.

blocks.caption: People take part in a rally in Tel Aviv calling for the opposition to form a government with the Arab parties after last week’s general election. Photograph: Jamal Awad/Reuters

blocks.text: “The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, added that some “suspicions” were still under investigation, but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over Herzog also denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens, who turned out to vote at historic rates.

“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”

Herzog plays a key role in formation of the next government, by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, in an announcement that could come as early as Thursday evening.

A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Palestinian-led parties have said their priority is removing Netanyahu so are also expected to back him as the strongest contender to achieve that.

However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He also accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in a bid to hold on to power.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot has secured the public support of all the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Photograph: Paulina Patimer/JNA/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement, and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.

The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would allow harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Analyst Nadav Eyal warned that Israelis should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel,”

Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel, about 20% of the population, and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.

Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as the news of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.

“(The) Attorney General is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

articles.title: UK to deploy facial recognition in biggest-ever immigration crackdown
articles.summary:
Documents show Home Office developing programme to use technology for general immigration enforcement

The Home Office is preparing to deploy facial recognition technology at transport hubs…

blocks.text: The Home Office is preparing to deploy facial recognition technology at transport hubs and public events as part of the biggest immigration enforcement crackdown in British history.

Policy documents show the government has been developing a programme to deploy live facial recognition (LFR) cameras for “general immigration enforcement”, including non-criminal immigration offences.
The technology will be used to identify people “seeking to re-enter the UK unlawfully”, target those subject to removal action and to crack down on broader “immigration-related criminality”.

The Home Office states the cameras will be used to locate undocumented people so it can resolve their cases, which it says will reduce “disruption to the wider public compared to repeated enforcement visits at residential addresses or workplaces”.

The documents further suggest that people could be included on LFR watchlists for overstaying a visa without permission, or entering without leave, all of which are considered civil rather than criminal matters.
The developments are contained in a new guidance document for immigration enforcement officials published on 8 October and a data protection impact assessment made public later in the month.

Their publication follows the decision by Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, to double the budget for immigration enforcement and boost its workforce by 60% to allow “tens of thousands” more raids, arrests and deportations.
Between November last year and February, immigration enforcement conducted three trials of LFR technology at Holyhead port in north Wales.

The trials were narrowly focused on locating people travelling to the UK from Ireland through the common travel area in breach of deportation orders or on a warrant for “an immigration-related criminal offence”.

The documents suggests that, in the future, individuals “liable to detention under immigration legislation” and who have “failed to comply with immigration conditions of entry or stay” could also be put on a watchlist. The LFR project “has now moved into the formal delivery phase”, it is said.

Locations where immigration enforcement could deploy facial recognition cameras have also been expanded to include “proactive” deployments at transport hubs and at “specific” events which are “expected to increase footfall at a location”, although no specific geography is named.

A list of potential higher risk deployments includes locations with “heightened community sensitivity”. When the Home Office was asked for clarity on what is meant by “events” or “sensitive” locations, it refused to comment.

A spokesperson confirmed that it is “considering further trials” of LFR by immigration enforcement officers and that it was “actively exploring the potential benefits, implications, and future use of the technology”.

The new policy document states anyone under the age of 18 will not be included on a watchlist. Earlier this year it was revealed that the Home Office had continued to use an AI facial-age estimation tool despite knowing it had misidentified migrant children as adults.
after newsletter promotion

Campaigners have warned the “secretive” expansion is a “huge and shocking escalation of mass surveillance” and highlighted the well-documented bias towards misidentifying people of colour when used at some settings.

Griff Ferris, spokesperson for the Joint Council for the Welfare of Immigrants, said immigration enforcement already employed tactics that “persecute and terrorise migrant communities” and that giving it more power to use a “racist mass surveillance tool in public places is frightening”.

Sarah Lasoye, of the Open Rights Group, said immigration enforcement “appear to be giving themselves the green light to expand use of highly controversial facial recognition technologies without scrutiny, transparency or public consent”.
She said: “Immigration enforcement and police forces are exploiting an absence of national legislation regulating uses of AI technologies, including facial recognition, in the public sector”.

The policy documents claim the use of LFR by immigration enforcement “is subject to external oversight, including by the biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner and the Information Commissioner’s Office”.

The biometrics and surveillance camera commissioner, William Webster, told Liberty Investigates, which first uncovered the new policy documents, that he was not consulted on the policy and clarified that the use of LFR for immigration purposes falls outside of his remit.

He added that the “proliferation of LFR into different service contexts does raise important questions about the scope of existing regulatory oversight,” which he hopes will be addressed in the forthcoming legislative framework for facial recognition.

articles.title: US midterm elections 2026: live results from Senate, House and governor races in all 50 states
articles.summary: With many seats still to come in, the Democrats have taken control of the Senate, House and several key governorships. Find live updating results in full here
articles.byline: Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

blocks.text: Democrats*
*includes 2 independents
33/35 races called
Democrats
218 to win
First results expected after 18.00 EST (15.00 PST, 23.00 GMT, 10.00 AEST)

Most US election seats are reliably won by one party, so control of Congress comes down to a few competitive "battleground" seats. Experts track these to predict overall results; if a party wins seats they were expected to lose, it often signals a successful night. In the charts below, blue shapes on the right signal a good night for the Democrats, and red shapes on the left signal that the Republicans have done well.
Senate
See full results
Before the election, the Cook Report classified six Senate races as genuine "toss-ups". The Democrats need to win at least three of these, alongside the other races they are expected to win.
Likely DemocratLikely Dem.
Lean DemocratLean Dem.
Toss-upToss-up
Lean RepublicanLean Rep.
Likely RepublicanLikely Rep.
House

Democrats were favoured in enough House seats to take the chamber without winning any of the 18 seats the Cook Political Report classed as “toss-ups”. If they won every seat they were expected to win, they would comfortably win a majority. The balance of power rested on whether Democrats would hold the 18 seats rated “lean Democratic”. Republicans, favoured in 195 seats, would have needed to sweep all 18 toss-ups and flip five Democratic-leaning seats to win.

Thirty-three of the 100 members of the upper chamber were being elected regularly this year, along with two other special elections. Republicans had the Senate majority before the election. Senators serve six-year terms.
Election explained
Loading map...

Republicans were defending a majority in the 435-member House. Democrats held 212 House seats and needed 218 to win control. Members of the House of Representatives serve two-year terms and face re-election every even year.

Gubernatorial elections were taking place in 36 states, as well as three territories. Republicans and Democrats held 18 of these state governorships each before the election. Three incumbent governors were retiring.
34/36 races called
How the elections work
The US legislature, Congress, has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate.
How is the House of Representatives elected and how do they work?
The lower chamber, the House of Representatives, has 435 voting seats, each representing a district of roughly similar size. There are elections for each of these seats every two years.

The speaker of the House is the chamber’s presiding officer, elected by the representatives. The House has several exclusive powers, such as the power to initiate revenue bills, impeach federal officials and elect the president in the case of an electoral college tie.
How is the Senate elected and how do they work?

The upper chamber, the Senate, has 100 members, who sit for six-year terms. One-third of the seats come up for election in each two-year cycle. Each state has two senators, regardless of its population; this means that Wyoming, with a population of less than 600,000, carries the same weight as California, with almost 40 million.

Most legislation needs to pass both chambers to become law, but the Senate has some important other functions, notably approving senior presidential appointments, for instance to the supreme court. The Senate also has the sole power to provide advice to the president, consent to ratify treaties and try impeachment cases for federal officials referred to it by the House.

In most states, the candidate with the most votes on election day wins the seat. However, Georgia and Louisiana require the winning candidate to garner 50% of votes cast; if no one does, they hold a runoff election between the top two candidates.

Maine and Alaska use ranked-choice voting as opposed to the first past the post voting system in congressional elections. Voters rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate receives a majority of first-choice votes, the least-supported candidate is eliminated and their ballots are transferred to each voter’s next-ranked candidate. This continues until a candidate wins a majority.

In some states, an election can feature two candidates from the same party. Under top-two or “jungle” primary systems, candidates from all parties compete in the same primary and the two receiving the most votes advance, regardless of party. The congressional election candidates could both be Democrats or both be Republicans.

Florida and Ohio are having ‘special elections’ for the Senate because the previous holders of their seats – Marco Rubio and JD Vance – resigned to join the executive branch following the 2024 presidential election.
How are governors elected and how do they work?
Governors are elected by direct vote in their states. The candidate with the highest number of votes is declared the winner.
In every state, the executive branch is led by a governor. They serve for four years in office, with the exception of Vermont and New Hampshire where tenures are two years long.
Governors are responsible for implementing state laws, and have a range of powers available to them such as executive orders, executive budgets and legislative proposals and vetoes.
How are the results reported?

The election results on this page are reported by the Associated Press. AP will “call” the winner in a state when it determines that the trailing candidate has no path to victory. This can happen before 100% of votes in a state have been counted.
Estimates for the total vote in each state are also provided by AP. The numbers update throughout election night and in the following days, as more data on voter turnout becomes available.
Antonio Voce, Seán Clarke, Ed Gargan, Anna Leach and Ashley Kirk

articles.title: A nuclear Philippines in six years? OECD’s nuclear chief isn’t convinced.
articles.summary: The head of the OECD's Nuclear Energy Agency casts doubt on the Philippines' 2032 nuclear target, saying that getting its first reactor operating will likely take longer than six years

blocks.text: The head of the OECD's Nuclear Energy Agency casts doubt on the Philippines' 2032 nuclear target, saying that getting its first reactor operating will likely take longer than six years

items: The OECD-NEA director-general stated that the Philippines is unlikely to have its first nuclear reactor operational by 2032, citing the lengthy development process and the nascent regulatory environment.
The Department of Energy's draft guidelines suggest initial electricity deliveries from nuclear projects may start in 2038, six years later than the government's original target.
Public support for nuclear energy in the Philippines is relatively high, but concerns about nuclear waste management and community acceptance remain significant challenges.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines is unlikely to have its first nuclear reactor operating by 2032, according to the head of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Nuclear Energy Agency (OECD-NEA), who warned that developing a nuclear power plant would take longer than six years.

“I don’t think you’re going to have the first reactor operating in six years. It simply takes longer than that. You might have a decision in six years,” OECD-NEA director-general William Magwood told reporters on Wednesday, November 4.

“There’s a lot of discussions that have to be had between governments, between the utility and vendors. These take years to go through,” he added. “And the regulator is still very nascent. It’s just getting started. So no, it won’t happen in five or six years. But it will certainly happen within the foreseeable future if things stay on track.”

The international nuclear expert’s assessment comes less than a month after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed that the government’s target of introducing 1,200 megawatts (MW) of nuclear capacity by 2032 was achievable.

That timeline is already being reconsidered by Energy Secretary Sharon Garin. In addition, the Department of Energy’s (DOE) draft nuclear power capacity tender guidelines is already framed more conservatively, with initial electricity deliveries in 2038, six years later than Marcos’ endorsed target. This timetable applies to projects under the proposed tender though, meaning earlier projects through other arrangements may also be possible.

blocks.caption: TIMELINE. DOE’s timeline in its draft nuclear capacity tender as of September 2026 shows a first target delivery date of 2038.

blocks.text: “The draft nuclear energy tender does indicate already that delivery starts in 2038. And we’ve also gone on record in statements that we will stick to what’s in the plan,” DOE Director IV Patrick Aquino told reporters. “As you know, nuclear power projects takes a long time, takes a lot of push, so we are still not officially changing. We’re still hopeful on getting it done.”

With the ambitious goal, the DOE has been busy hosting forums and courting nuclear experts, suppliers, and developers. However, some early roadblocks have already appeared, with the Philippine Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (PhilATOM) still awaiting the appointment of its leadership and its unfinished implementing rules and regulation.

Beyond setting up the regulator, Aquino said the DOE was pursuing capacity-building initiatives, including human resource development and technical cooperation with countries that already operate nuclear facilities.

Magwood, however, warned that recruiting qualified personnel remains a “very big struggle” even in OECD countries, with nuclear regulators requiring specialists in engineering, science, geology, and other fields.

blocks.caption: Filipinos helped build UAE’s nuclear plant. PH talent may soon do the same back home.

blocks.text: Then there is the issue of getting the public to accept nuclear energy, with its risks and long-lasting waste.
So far, DOE surveys have shown relatively strong nationwide support for nuclear energy, with approval rising from 79% in 2019 to 82% in 2024.

Aquino said acceptance in communities being considered for nuclear development has also been relatively high, ranging from 60% to 90% depending on the location. Potential sites assessed include Bataan, Palawan, Masbate, Pangasinan, and Camarines Norte, while another nationwide survey is being prepared.
Still, Magwood cautioned that support could vary between communities.

“People in Philippines seem to be ready to have this conversation and to see where it takes them,” he said. “There’s a lot of support in some parts of the country and in other parts, maybe not as much. That’s pretty typical.”
Among the concerns is nuclear waste, which can remain dangerously radioactive long after it is removed from a reactor.

Magwood said there already exists technology to safely store spent nuclear fuel in specialized containers for decades before eventual disposal in geological repositories. However, he acknowledged that despite the technological advances made, nuclear waste is still “a very emotional topic,” especially for host communities.
While expressing confidence that the Philippines could manage nuclear waste, Magwood acknowledged that the country has yet to determine its approach to final disposal.
“The cost comes at the final disposal. But the Philippines hasn’t decided on that yet so it’s hard to put a cost estimate to it,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: More than 900 academics urge UK to reverse decision to bar Andreas Malm
articles.summary:
Blocking Swedish writer’s entry for event with Palestine Action co-founder is attack on free expression, letter says

More than 900 academics have voiced their opposition to the government’s…

blocks.text: More than 900 academics have voiced their opposition to the government’s decision to block the climate academic Andreas Malm from entering the UK, warning that the move represents “a grave violation of academic freedom and freedom of expression”.

Malm, the author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline and a leading climate scholar, was prevented from entering the UK last week by the Home Office after being told that his presence in the UK “may not be considered to be conducive to the public good”.

He had been due to attend an academic conference on Wednesday, appear on the BBC, and participate in a public discussion organised by the publication Tribune alongside Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the proscribed organisation Palestine Action.
Hundreds of academics have signed an open letter voicing their concern at the move and calling on the government to overturn the decision.

“The ability of scholars to travel, exchange ideas and participate in public debate – including on politically contentious issues – is fundamental to a free and democratic society,” the letter says. “Excluding academics because of their political views or the topics they discuss sets a dangerous precedent and risks creating a chilling effect on academic and public discourse.”

Malm, an associate professor at Lund University in Sweden and an internationally recognised climate academic, said he had been “kept in the dark” by the UK’s immigration authorities over the reasons for his electronic travel authorisation (ETA) being revoked, but said he suspected it was because of his plans to appear on a panel alongside Ammori from Palestine Action.

Speaking to the BBC earlier this week, he said: “I cannot see any other explanation than the scheduled appearance of me on stage for a panel on Wednesday evening in London, together with Huda Ammori. That … makes me somehow a terrorist or associated with terrorism, and therefore barred from travelling to the UK. That’s pretty scandalous.”

He said the move was “just a very small part of a major trend: this drift into authoritarianism that is targeting the Palestine movement, the climate movement, and others who oppose the destructive forces that are in control of this world.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Cancelling or refusing an ETA can take place for a range of reasons, including where there are concerns that an individual poses a threat to public safety or seeks to spread extremism.
“It is not a ban on coming to the UK. Those in this position can still apply for a visa, enabling further consideration of circumstances and suitability for entry to the UK.”
The letter has so far been signed by more than 1,400 individuals from over 250 academic institutions, including some of the world’s leading universities.
Fabian Dablander, an assistant professor at the London School of Economics, who initiated the letter, said the numbers showed the strength of feeling in the academic community.

“The letter quickly attracted hundreds of signatures, reflecting the academic community’s deep concern about the threat this decision poses to academic freedom and the UK’s reputation as a place for open intellectual debate,” he said.

articles.summary:
German carmaker slashes profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year in face of competition from China

The German carmaker BMW has issued its second profit warning in a year, blaming…

blocks.text: The German carmaker BMW has issued its second profit warning in a year, blaming the costs of a restructuring programme including significant job losses in the face of continuing competition from China.

The company is the latest to issue a profit downgrade in the German car sector, with Mercedes-Benz last week cutting its profit outlook. Western automakers have struggled to keep pace with lower-cost domestic rivals in China, which has led to reduced sales there and a rise in exports to Europe.

BMW signalled a potential for losses after slashing its profit margin to between -0.5% and 0.5% this year but blamed fourth-quarter costs tied to the restructuring that includes 8,000 job cuts in its home market. At the beginning of the year, BMW had still considered a margin of 4-6% would be possible.
It reported an 11% drop in third-quarter pre-tax earnings on Wednesday to €2.1bn (£1.75bn).
Sales in China fell 22% in the first nine months of the year but BMW said this was in line with the broader downturn ⁠in that market.

“Current developments in our industry call for decisiveness and swift implementation. We will therefore specifically intensify and accelerate structural measures,” the chief executive Milan Nedeljković said.
China “remains a key focus”, Nedeljković added, with the group’s Neue Klasse ​revival of its model offering beginning in ​China this month with the launch of the iX3.
BMW follows Volkswagen with painful restructuring costs caused by the rapidly changing market.

Because of the rapid launch of its new generation of electric vehicles, the company is writing off parts of its previous vehicle and technology generations and pricing in the costs of the redundancy programme.
The operating ‌margin in BMW’s core ‌automotive business narrowed to 3.4%, beating analysts’ forecast of 3.1% but declining from 5.2% a year earlier.
Excluding restructuring charges, the margin would be above 2%, within its previous forecast range, the company said.
after newsletter promotion
BMW said it planned to cut management functions more quickly under its restructuring drive.
Revenue fell 6% to €30.4bn in the third quarter, hurt by the declining sales in China.

Although BMW’s ​rival Mercedes-Benz also reported lower profits in the third quarter, Porsche rebounded slightly but only after steep charges last year as it overhauls its model lineup and retreats from China.

articles.title: Firework noise limit should be drastically cut to protect wild animals, UK government told
articles.summary:
Ministers urged to go further than proposed cut to 110 decibels to ease acute stress on birds and others animals

Campaigners are calling on the government to protect the welfare of wild…

blocks.text: Campaigners are calling on the government to protect the welfare of wild animals by cutting the maximum noise level of fireworks sold to the public from 120 to 90 decibels.

The Center for Wild Animal Welfare (CWAW) has said lowering the limit to 90 decibels – which is about one-eighth of the loudness of 120 decibels – would help to protect millions of wild animals from acute stress by reducing the area over which a firework disturbs surrounding wildlife.
This would help prevent incidents of harm, such as mass temporary displacement and fatal collisions among birds, that can occur during fireworks displays, it says.

It comes after the UK government recently consulted on proposals to lower the maximum noise level of fireworks sold to the public from 120 decibels to 110 decibels, which equate to their loudness being approximately halved.
But CWAW said the proposed limit did not go far enough and cutting it to 90 decibels would leave the area disturbed by each firework about a hundred times smaller than under the government’s plan.

Richard Parr, CWAW’s director, said: “Sound travels, and a loud firework can penetrate surprisingly far – up to 10km. Because decibels work on a [logarithmic] scale, each 10-decibel cut to the limit reduces the area affected by the noise by 10 times.”

Parr said that while many people were aware of the distress caused by fireworks to pets, there was not enough awareness of how such loud noises affected wild animals. “There’s no reason to think that wild animals would be any less affected than pets,” he said. “It might even be worse because it’s completely unnatural. It’s surprising, stressing, and disturbing for their natural rhythms of life to be suddenly and very unexpectedly disrupted.
“Particularly for prey animals, who have evolved to be cautious and are naturally jumpy, these random, unannounced bangs are terrifying.”

Rebecca Machin, a wildlife expert at the RSPCA, said she shared CWAW’s concerns about the impact of fireworks on wildlife. “Fireworks and their debris can disturb a range of wild animals, particularly birds, causing suffering and distress,” she said. “Depending on the distance from the explosive and the noise level, impacts include disrupted migration, elevated stress hormones, and hazards from leftover firework debris.”

Research into the impact of fireworks on wild animals has found that birds experience particular harm during fireworks displays, including stress responses, mass temporary displacement and fatal collisions. On New Year’s Day in 2025, more than 1,000 birds were found dead near a hiking trail in Bulgaria, just over a kilometre from a site where fireworks had been set off, after panicked birds flew into trees and each other.

The government consultation came after concerns about the noise and availability of fireworks were aired in a parliamentary debate in January, with two petitions gaining more than 180,000 signatures each. Alongside the noise limit, the consultation looked at expanding the list of fireworks banned for general sale and reviewing the rules on lower-risk products, including scrapping the age limit on Christmas crackers.

New Zealand introduced a 90-decibel limit on consumer fireworks in 2008. It also reduced the number of days they can be sold and raised the minimum purchase age from 14 to 18, in line with the UK and most other countries. However, the UK government consultation noted there had been concerns that the noise testing system could be gamed because a 90-decibel limit was difficult to define precisely in legislation.

In response to the calls for a 90-decibel limit, a spokesperson for the British Fireworks Association said: “We are aware of reports that sudden, unexpected noise from fireworks and other sources can disturb birds and other wildlife, and we take those concerns seriously. People should consider where and when they set off fireworks and take steps to minimise disturbance.

“However, we do not believe the case has been made for reducing the noise limit to 90 decibels. Any change should be based on clear evidence of its likely benefits and take account of unintended consequences, including the risk of people turning to illegal fireworks. We favour better enforcement of existing laws, alongside a national campaign to encourage safe and considerate use of fireworks.”

articles.title: DA admits submitting wrong coordinates for 8 proposed 2027 farm-to-market roads
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Wednesday admitted that eight farm-to-market road (FMR) projects included in its proposed 2027 budget contained incorrect coordinates due to encoding and…

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 7:38pm

The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Wednesday admitted that eight farm-to-market road (FMR) projects included in its proposed 2027 budget contained incorrect coordinates due to supposed "encoding and geotagging errors."
DA Assistant Secretary for Operations U-Nichols Manalo disclosed this during a hearing of the House agriculture and food committee on the government's response to El Niño.
Manalo said the eight projects were among the 1,669 FMR projects nationwide included in the DA's proposed budget under the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

“We’d like to inform the committee that the 1,669 farm-to-market road projects are within the NEP (National Expenditure Program) [proposed to the House]. Hindi iyon dun sa sinasabi nating inserted farm-to-market road projects,” Manalo said.
(These 1,669 FMR projects were not among those inserted by lawmakers.)

Manalo made the clarification after budget watchdog People’s Budget Coalition flagged provisions in the proposed 2027 national budget, which the House had approved on third and final reading, over allegedly incorrect project coordinates.
The group earlier cited hundreds of farm-to-market road (FMR) projects, questioning their locations and the transparency of the project allocations.
The group reported that some projects had coordinates pointing to bodies of water, including the Celebes Sea and the Philippine Rise.
Manalo attributed the errors in the eight FMR projects to “encoding and geotagging errors.”
Camarines Sur 4th District Rep. Arnie Fuentebella urged the DA to acknowledge and correct the errors while the proposed national budget was still under deliberation in the Senate.
“I think you can still correct it,” Fuentebella said.
“We appreciate you acknowledging your mistake,” he added.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: First Thing: Democrats sweep into control of Congress after historic midterm victories
articles.summary: Both the House and Senate will be under Democratic control for the rest of Donald Trump’s term in office. Plus, the French Homer and Marge who found true love in real life

blocks.text: Good morning. Democrats have won control of Congress in a historic and dramatic “blue wave” in the midterm elections. The results have huge implications for the remaining two years of Donald Trump’s term in office, as Democrats flipped critical Republican seats across the country and also scored a string of victories in gubernatorial races and in districts that Republicans had tried to redraw to their advantage. Democrats have so far clinched 54 seats in the Senate and 225 House seats to take control of both chambers. The full results can be found here.

Rachel Leingang wrote in her analysis piece this morning: “Democrats of all stripes declared victory on Tuesday night: moderates, progressives, populists, Democratic socialists. And they won up and down the ballot. These victories will provide avenues for Democrats to hold Trump accountable and act as a functioning branch of government, something voters have said they’ve been missing in Trump 2.0.”
Here are the key headlines:

items: James Talarico won the US Senate race in Texas, breaking a 38-year drought for his party in the Republican stronghold.
Troy Jackson won Maine’s Senate race, toppling the five-term Republican incumbent, Susan Collins, in one of the biggest upsets.
Abdul El-Sayed, the doctor and progressive insurgent, made history in winning the closely watched US Senate race in Michigan to become the country’s first Muslim senator.
Jon Ossoff, cited as a potential presidential contender in 2028, has been re-elected to the Senate in Georgia.
Chris Pappas, the four-term Democratic congressman, won New Hampshire’s US Senate race, making him the first out gay man to serve in the upper chamber.
Sherrod Brown will return to the US Senate, as Ohio’s voters rejected the incumbent, Jon Husted.

Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who campaigned on healthcare affordability, won the race for US Senate in South Carolina, making her the first Democrat to represent the state in the Senate for more than a quarter century.
The former governor Roy Cooper will be the first Democrat to represent North Carolina in the Senate in 10 years, after defeating Michael Whatley.
Adam Hamilton won in Kansas to become the state’s first Democratic senator since 1932.
Gina Hinojosa defeated the three-term governor Greg Abbott, shattering the Republican grip on the highest and most powerful executive office in Texas.
The Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, will become the first Black female governor in the US after winning the gubernatorial race in Georgia.
Deb Haaland, the interior secretary under Joe Biden, has been elected governor of New Mexico and will become the first Native American woman to govern a US state.
Rob Sand has been elected governor of Iowa. Josh Turek won the US Senate race there.
Amy Acton was elected governor of Ohio after an ugly contest in which her rival Vivek Ramaswamy spent millions of dollars on deeply personal attack ads featuring her estranged mother.
Xavier Becerra, the Democratic former health and human services secretary, was elected governor of California.
The Republican Ashley Moody fended off a challenge from Angie Nixon, a Democratic socialist, to win Florida’s special election and retain her seat in the US Senate.
The Trump-endorsed Republican Byron Donalds will be the next governor of Florida, and its first Black leader, after defeating the Democrat David Jolly.

articles.title: Woman charged over alleged stalking and attempted extortion of Greens senator Jordon Steele-John
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Police will allege the woman, 40, is the former partner of Steele-John and she is expected to face court in Perth on Thursday

A 40-year-old woman has been…

blocks.text: A 40-year-old woman has been arrested and charged by Western Australian police for allegedly stalking and attempting to extort the Greens senator Jordon Steele-John.

WA police said on Wednesday detectives from the family violence investigation squad charged the Perth woman with one count of aggravated stalking with intent to intimidate and one count of demanding property by written threats, commonly known as extortion.
WA police will allege the woman is a former partner of Steele-John.
The woman is due to appear in a Perth magistrates court on Thursday morning.
A spokesperson for Steele-John said: “The senator won’t be commenting on this investigation further at this time.”

Steele-John did not attend parliament last week after a group of Greens members sent a three-page letter to the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, urging an investigation into allegations that Steele-John had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
In a 2,400-word statement following a report by the Nine newspapers, Steele-John denied all the allegations made against him in the letter.
These complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.

articles.title: Ramon Ang’s youngest son Jacob joins his family on Ginebra board
articles.summary: With the youngest Ang’s appointment, there are now four Ang family members on Ginebra's nine-member board

blocks.text: With the youngest Ang’s appointment, there are now four Ang family members on Ginebra's nine-member board

MANILA, Philippines – Jacob Paolo Ang, the youngest son of San Miguel Corporation (SMC) chairman Ramon Ang, has joined the board of Ginebra San Miguel where three of his other family members already have a seat.

Jacob was elected director following the death last September of retired military general Leo Alvez, Ginebra said in a disclosure on Wednesday, November 4. Alvez had been a director of Ginebra since April 2002.

With the youngest Ang’s appointment, there are now four Ang family members on Ginebra’s nine-member board. The board now includes Jacob; his father Ramon Ang, who is Ginebra’s president and SMC’s chairman and CEO; and his siblings John Paul, SMC’s vice chairman, president, and chief operating officer; and Cecile, an SMC director and vice president of New NAIA Infra Corporation.

Just in his mid-20s, Jacob’s corporate experience revolves around San Miguel’s automotive businesses. He has served as president of BMW distributor SMC Asia Car Distributors Corporation since 2025 and as director and chief planning officer of Ferrari distributor Velocita Motors since 2023.
He has also served as executive assistant to the SMC chairman, his father.
Jacob graduated from Ateneo de Manila University in 2023 with a degree in European Studies and completed a leadership and management development program in 2024.
Before working for the family conglemerate, he was a championship kart racer.
Ginebra’s disclosure did not list any previous experience in liquor manufacturing or distribution.

Under the company’s corporate governance manual, directors must be at least 21 years old, have a college degree or sufficient management experience, and own at least 5,000 company shares. Jacob meets these minimum requirements, with Ginebra disclosing that he owns 5,000 shares. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Google launches AI-based shopping in Canada, with a new ‘universal’ checkout cart
articles.summary: Google launched a new online shopping tool in Canada on Wednesday, allowing complete purchases via chat with its AI agent.

image.caption: Google launched its new AI-based shopping tool in Canada on Wednesday, including a new ‘universal’ checkout cart. (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar, File) (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar)

blocks.text: Google launched a new tool in Canada on Wednesday that will let users buy things with an AI chatbot, essentially eliminating the role of the e-commerce checkout cart.
American users gained access to the tool, called the Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), on Oct. 15.
The feature is the California-based company's latest salvo in a fierce battle to control e-commerce, as tech companies race to turn conversational AI into digital points of sale.

items: BMO, CIBC, RBC, TD Bank block personal AI agents, citing safety and security

blocks.text: While retail giants like Amazon and Walmart have introduced AI assistants that are effectively confined to their own platforms, Google is competing with agents like Meta’s Muse that can work across different online sites.

Both companies — Meta and Alphabet — are seeking to become the universal checkout counter for internet retailers, meant to help shoppers avoid re-entering their payment details across multiple storefronts.

As of Wednesday, shoppers can buy items they discover across Google Search through a conversation with its Gemini chatbot. Purchases will be processed through Google Pay using shipping and payment details saved in Google Wallet. The individual retailer, not Google, remains the seller of record, taking full legal responsibility for fulfilling the order.
Eric Morris, head of retail at Google Canada, calls the new feature "a new way for Canadians to shop."
Why banks are banning AI agents
For now, Google’s offering is limited to a handful of Canadian retail partners — Lululemon, Shoppers Drug Mart, Simons and select Shopify merchants, with more expected in the new year.
Shopify is both Google's partner and its rival. The Ottawa-based company helped build Google’s in-chat checkout, even as it rolls out competing AI shopping tools of its own.
"AI is changing the way that consumers search," Google Canada's Morris told CBC News.

And Google, best known for its search engine, is acutely exposed to that change. Last Thursday, shares of its parent company Alphabet plunged by double-digits, erasing roughly $500 billion US in market value in a single trading session, after the company booked weaker-than-expected search and advertising revenue.

"In the old days, you might go to Google and search for running tights, and you’d get 10 blue links and pictures of different products," Morris said, describing the company's legacy search experience.
AI agents could change how you use the internet
Shopping with AI is a lot more conversational, he says. That same query for running shoes to a chatbot might go something like this:
If a user asks, "What are the best running types for a cold, snowy Toronto winter?"
"In that chat interface, you'd be presented with a series of options and products based on what you were searching for, and our ability to predict the products that most likely match," he said.
He notes that access to Google's UCP service will be free for retailers.
Choices 'more constrained' with AI shopping

A leading Canadian policy expert says this new style of shopping gives companies like Google and Meta access to transaction and purchase data that would otherwise be in the hands of individual retailers.
Vass Bednar, managing director at the Canadian SHIELD Institute for Public Policy, also questions whether AI can be trusted to prioritize specific consumer needs, like finding the lowest price.
"What the research is starting to show is that in an AI shopping context, choice is more constrained than on the open web," she said.
"The potential risk or trade-off is that you’re not actually getting the best quality or cheapest price.… You’re getting an offer that is served to you through an advertising relationship."
He used Meta’s AI agent Muse for Marketplace sales. Then it set one up behind his back
However, a representative from the Retail Council of Canada said the feature can allow budget-conscious consumers to find deals and compare prices more easily.
"I think it's a positive, because it helps people feel more prepared," said Santo Ligotti, the council’s vice-president of membership and marketing.

"There's always gonna be the fear of inaccurate information, if it's sponsored or biased … but the more that Canadians use it, and the more the companies are allowing themselves to be more discoverable on AI, the more I think we're going to see this as just another tool in the toolkit to help people plan on how they want to spend."

However, while agents may help people find items quicker, users should not assume they are always being provided the absolute lowest price, said David Soberman, a marketing professor at the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management.
"I definitely recommend that people do a lot of cross-checking, because sometimes these AI agents miss things."
Retailers becoming 'passive players,' says U of T prof
Like Bednar, Soberman sees more control shifting into the hands of big tech.
"The amalgamation of a search engine with AI agents in general has made the retailers sort of passive players in this whole ecosystem," he said.
Google Canada expects 59 per cent of Canadians to use an AI tool for their holiday shopping this year. Figures from Deloitte and PwC are softer — 39 per cent, and 28 per cent, respectively.
Last week, some of Canada’s largest banks announced plans to block third-party AI agents from accessing their clients' online bank accounts and other information, citing safety and security concerns.
LISTEN | How AI agents could change shopping:
Just Asking46:23Agentic AI could change how you shop
Morris says Google isn’t worried.
"It's still humans making the purchase. No one else," he said. "The way it works is that the transaction is secure and encrypted. You'd buy securely using Google Pay."
Meanwhile, Nick Engel, Lululemon’s senior vice-president of global digital experience, says he expects agentic AI shopping will be a hit with fans of the Vancouver-based activewear brand.
"I think we are going to see a wave of guests using [large language models] for both discovery, and then for shopping, this holiday season," he said.
"Banks are obviously going to have very different standards than retailers."

articles.title: Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's gorgeous remake retains the original's soul
articles.summary: Nearly 30 years after the original, Nintendo has remade The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. It’s an unquestionable fan favourite that’s shinier, but retains the soul of a game that isn’t made like…

image.caption: The protagonist Link, all grown up and glowed up in the new remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo Switch 2. (Nintendo)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Nearly 30 years after the original, Nintendo has remade The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. It’s an unquestionable fan favourite that’s shinier, but retains the soul of a game that isn’t made like this anymore.
Improved controls, modern visuals do justice to the seminal 1998 adventure game

If you loved the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, chances are you don't remember the moments that were clunky, hard to control and kind of ugly, because the good stuff outstripped the bad by a longshot.

Now, Nintendo has remade and rebuilt the 1998 classic from the ground up, for the Switch 2 console. In doing so, they've managed to recreate the good memories from this iconic game, but with modern improvements to the visuals, responsive controls and much more.

In other words, they've avoided making this stroll down memory lane a cringe-inducing slog. The end result will feel like a comforting hug to many gamers, but its world will welcome anyone who hasn't visited before.
Ocarina of Time is better than you remember
It looks way better

What hasn't changed is the classic story of the balance between good and evil. Ocarina of Time tells the interweaving tale of Zelda, a princess burdened with dark, prophetic dreams; Ganondorf, the manipulative power-hungry thief; and Link, a boy with a mark of destiny who must grow up quick — figuratively and literally, thanks to time travel — to meet the challenge.
As Link, you still navigate the Kingdom of Hyrule: a beautiful, wide world full of puzzles, weapons and enemies.
The blocky, polygonal graphics of the original version meant some of this epic storytelling had to be done in our imagination.
But on the Switch 2, the rays of the sun shine, the dust flows, the water glistens and the characters — even the weird ones — have gestures, emotions and faces with more discernable features.
Link stands in front of the Great Deku Tree. Fireflies, light and mist swirl about, showing off the graphical sea change from the original to the remake. (Nintendo)

From the stained-glass texture of your fairy companion Navi to the latex skin of the fish-like Zora people, Ocarina feels like it's giving you reasons to pay attention to details in this era of second-screen distractions. There are no graphical hiccups or bathroom-break loading screen times here.
The tools and weapons essential to your journey are colourful and responsive, from deflecting monster projectiles with your shield to the hissing of a lit bomb that you'd better throw soon.
Unlike the original, which would automatically throw Link over pits and edges, jumping now has a button, giving the player more control over combat and traversal.
It sounds the same (that's a good thing)
Speaking of those tools, they are a driving force in one of the best parts to any Zelda adventure: the sound design.

The shlink of a sword, the hyaah of our otherwise silent protagonist, the clunk-thunk of iron boots and the creak of opening a treasure chest are all still here. Nintendo has done little to improve the sound effects other than making them sound less tinny.
Yes, that includes the symphony of squelching as you navigate the insides of Jabu-Jabu, a giant fish-like creature.
Link holding the titular Ocarina of Time, with his fairy companion Navi beside him. (Nintendo)

The titular ocarina is still a satisfying woodwind to play, but now you can hum the tunes in case you forget (or don't want to bother remembering) the exact note combinations. Songs are key to game progression, and if you don't want to sing aloud, simple button presses will also work.

The musical score is just as lovely and supportive of the grand adventure as before. The castanets and guitar got me vibing through the deserts of Gerudo Valley, and I loved how the tempo slowed down as night fell over the canyon.

New voice acting and a slightly reworked script helps boost moments so you're not just mashing buttons to hurry along boxes of text on the screen. Thankfully, the melodrama of that acting and writing never overstay their welcome. Ganondorf is wonderful in brief menacing monologues, but the forest dwelling would-be-tough-guy Mido steals the show.
It feels bigger, but is actually faster

Ocarina benefits from quick pacing elsewhere, too. While it takes up more than 20 gigabytes of storage — more than 2023's Tears of the Kingdom — this adventure isn't heavily beset with tasks and side quests.

Early on, you might think the tall, vast, gorgeous world before you feels endless. But you'll quickly realize that few treasures are hidden in the walls, and slashing at shrubs won't uncover much more than a couple of rupees.
Link gets ready to ride his horse Epona. Though your horse helps the speed of traversing the map, it's a tiny world compared to modern Zelda games. (Nintendo)
But that's a good thing.

The last two Zelda games on the Switch — Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom — took the franchise into an exhaustive open world, a feature of modern games that try to keep you in these environments for dozens of hours.

Ocarina of Time, however, is focused on good level design and clever mechanics to get through them. In the later temples, for example, it's all about switching between your tools to figure out a path through a unique set of rooms.
That means this game doesn't take as long to beat — and this may be the one downside to staying true to its roots.

What used to be semi-challenging puzzles in the original now feel a little dated and are over before you know it. The same goes for the epic set-piece boss battles that you can finish in a few hits, making you wonder what all that dungeon-crawling was for. (Thankfully, another modern improvement is the ability to replay boss fights for bragging rights.)
But like some good, old memories, it's not worth interrogating. The Ocarina of Time remake is short, sweet and worth reliving — or worth making the memories for the first time.
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time releases Nov. 5 on the Switch 2 and retails for $84.99.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Anand Ram is a reporter and producer with CBC's science and climate unit. He's worked as a reporter covering technology, business and the environment and as a producer with The National.

articles.title: ‘The point was to dehumanise’: London Holocaust archive examines world’s first ‘viral’ antisemitism scandal
articles.summary:
Dreyfus affair has echoes of how anti-Jewish hatred manifests itself today, say curators at Weiner Library

It was the world’s first experience of antisemitism “gone viral”, said Barbara…

blocks.text: It was the world’s first experience of antisemitism “gone viral”, said Barbara Warnock, a co-director of the oldest Holocaust archive, the Wiener Holocaust Library in London.

It was 1894 and printing presses were faster than ever before. France’s prohibitive censorship laws had been lifted, and then along came the Dreyfus affair: a public shouting match that followed the wrongful conviction for treason of Alfred Dreyfus, a 36-year-old French army captain.

The clash between those insistent on Dreyfus’s guilt, as a Jewish man deemed to have a questionable allegiance to the French republic, and his outraged defenders triggered a deluge of newspaper specials, bespoke journals, posters and other polemics.

blocks.caption: Alfred Dreyfus, who was exonerated 120 years ago.  Photograph: Wiener Holocaust Library Collections

blocks.text: A florid sample of the outpouring – including a British newspaper’s special edition, heavily coloured by an anti-French agenda – will go on display this week in a new exhibition at the Wiener Holocaust Library, 120 years after Dreyfus’s exoneration, promotion and award of the Légion d’honneur.
“This is a very relevant topic for now,” Warnock said at a preview of the exhibition. “And so there are maybe some interesting echoes in terms of how antisemitism manifests itself today.”

The Wiener Holocaust Library was founded by Alfred Wiener, grandfather to the Conservative peer Daniel Finkelstein. He fled Germany for the Netherlands in 1933 after the rise of the Nazis, and then escaped from Amsterdam to London in 1938, bringing with him an extensive collection of documents chronicling the rise of antisemitism.

Among the 40 or so Dreyfus exhibits on display are pieces that Wiener sourced, but there are others collected in the intervening decades by the library and a haul that is on long-term loan from Birkbeck, University of London.

The intention is to bring to life the toxic debate that split France the 1890s and early 1900s as Dreyfus languished in solitary confinement on the notorious Devil’s Island penal colony off French Guiana. Among the most eye-catching of the exhibits is a large poster in which Arthur Ranc, a leftwing politician, writer and newspaper editor who supported Dreyfus, is caricatured as an alligator-like creature with razor-sharp teeth.

It was one among a series of such posters titled the Musée des Horreurs, said Clara Dijkstra, one of the curators of the exhibition. “They were published from autumn 1899 to 1900 and there are 45 to 50 versions of this and they all depict key figures who are pro-Dreyfus,” she said.

“The point was to dehumanise all these figures that were defending Dreyfus’s innocence. They are reflective of a relaxation of the press, but actually after a year of them being published the government finally decided they were too grotesque and shut down publication of them.”

A copy of the rightwing newspaper La Libre Parole, founded by Édouard Drumont, initiator of the Antisemitic League of France, is notable for its “grotesque antisemitic imagery on its cover”, said Dijkstra. “It had a large circulation and this paper was the first one to start reporting on the fact that Dreyfus was guilty and so broke the story in a way.”

The only English-language Dreyfus-themed publication in the Wiener collection is a special 45-page edition of a weekly illustrated newspaper, the Graphic, which carried as its front-page headline “Dreyfus the martyr” above an image of his apparent arrest.

“It is not necessarily highlighting the antisemitism, but they focus more on the kind of miscarriage of justice,” Dijkstra said. “Everything playing out as a courtroom drama. I think that really captured people’s attention.”

blocks.caption: The Psst...! illustration. Photograph: Wiener Holocaust Library Collections

blocks.text: One journal published in France specifically to cover the Dreyfus affair emerged in direct response to an open letter, titled J’Accuse, written by the novelist Émile Zola to the French president, Félix Faure, in 1898. He accused the French government of antisemitism and a cover-up. Zola was later convicted of libel and fled to England.

One image in the publication, titled Psst….!, shows a Prussian officer pulling the strings of a mask of Zola’s face, and behind it is a caricature of a Jewish man. “It is implying that Germans are behind it all, that there is a conspiracy,” Dijkstra said. “It is pretty much always the same message.”

items: The exhibition, J’accuse! Press, Polemic and the Dreyfus Affair, runs from 5 November to 19 March at the Wiener Holocaust Library.

articles.title: Wawira Njiru — Kenya's No. 1 school feeder honored with the German Africa Prize
articles.summary: From a small fundraiser to a big enterprise, Wawira Njiru's Kenyan school feeding scheme has been more successful than even she would have thought. She's now being awarded with the German Africa…

image.caption: Wawira Njiru, founder and CEO of Food4Education, receives the 2026 German Africa PrizeImage: Food4Education

blocks.text: From starting a modest fundraiser for 25 school children, Wawira Njiru has become a social entrepreneur with a staggering 6,000 staff on her payroll, feeding 600,000 kids in Kenya every day with her organization Food4Education (F4E) an engagement for which she is being honored with this year's German Africa Prize. How did this transformation come to pass?
The answer may be in her character. Stubborn and hard-working, that's how Njiru sees herself: "It's hard to tell me something is not possible."

Thinking back to how she began, she explained: "My dream then, my ambition was to feed 100 kids every day. I was 21 years old then, so also having an ambition of feeding 100 kids felt momentous. But now growing up, but also figuring out that you can do more, and just being obsessed with 'How much more can you do? How much more can you do,' led me here."
Wawira Njiru left her native Kenya after finishing school to study nutrition science in Adelaide, Australia.
Connecting the dots

"I knew a lot of kids back home were not getting the education they need. At that time, I was learning about the impact of food, and I didn't realize how powerful food was," Njiru said. "When you're doing a nutrition degree, that's when you really learn about the science behind food. And knowing that, especially for kids, it's so critical that they get nutritious meals."
When she found out her friends at the university often had a few dollars to spare and were looking for ways to contribute, she connected the dots and started her first fundraiser.

From there, the trajectory was set. But the road was rough at times for the young woman she was, Wawira explained. Some people didn't take her seriously. Others did. "You have to find your believers," Njiru found out. And furthermore: "You can't just go with your own name. You have to find someone to vouch for you or someone or something to validate your presence."

Her degree certainly helped. But still, many men looking for jobs just didn't seem confident in working for a young woman. This is why more than 70% of her employees today are women, Wawira Njiru said.
School meals at 3 cents, digitally tracked

Steadily pushing the limits, Food4Education now provides 19,000 schools across the country with a total of more than 600,000 meals every day. The system relies on a combination of funding: Helped by donations and government funding, parents are left with a small contribution, which in some cases amounts to 5 Kenyan shillings — a mere 3 US cents.

Payment is processed through the so-called "Tap-to-Eat" system. Every child has a wristband that is used to track each meal. Not only do the wristbands keep track of parents' payments, but they also help document how many meals are actually served. And if children don't pick up their meals, the team can find out why.

The model also relies on local sources wherever possible: about 80% of the food distributed by the organization comes from small-scale farmers. This way, school meals are freshly sourced — and farmers have a reliable market for selling their produce.
How Kenya is fighting hunger in schools
"For a long time, school meals were viewed as charity. We've proven that it's economic infrastructure," said 35-year-old Njiru.
Boosting attention and morale among school children

Does it pay out? It seems so. Data show that children at participating schools miss fewer classes, and they also perform better at school. "Food is everything," said Raphaera Kanya, director of a primary school in Kenya's capital Nairobi. "When your stomach has nothing, you cannot understand anything in class."

To Jane Nyambura, a pupil, the school feeding fosters equality at school. "There was a difference because there are some students who are finding accessing food very easy because their parents are available," she told DW. "There are others who can't afford food, and they feel as if it's unfair, as if there's something lacking in them. So it really demoralizes them and reduces their confidence."

blocks.caption: It's easier to concentrate and learn when you're well-fedImage: Andrew Wasike/DW

blocks.text: Wawira Njiru has already set her sights on the next benchmark: Reaching 1 million school children every day. She has every right, it seems, to be confident: "From 25 kids to now, I feel like there's not one challenge that we haven't overcome."
The Prize is awarded by the German Africa Foundation (DAS), a nonpartisan foundation dedicated to promoting a nuanced view of Africa in political circles and among the German public.

Since 1993, it has awarded the German Africa Prize to individuals from African countries whose ideas and work inspire solutions to global issues of the future beyond their countries of origin. The award has gone to outstanding individuals in Zimbabwe, Cameroon and Sierra Leone in recent years.
German Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan will present the German Africa Prize to Kenya's successful social entrepreneur on Wednesday evening.

articles.title: Very strong El Niño now present in tropical Pacific, says PAGASA
articles.summary: The El Niño phenomenon from the latter part of 2026 to the first half of 2027 is expected to be record-breaking in terms of heat, with temperatures across the Philippines expected to rise by 2C.

blocks.text: Published November 4, 2026 6:30pm
A very strong El Niño is now observed in the tropical Pacific, PAGASA on Wednesday said.
The El Niño phenomenon from the latter part of 2026 to the first half of 2027 is expected to be record-breaking in terms of heat, with temperatures across the Philippines expected to rise by 2C.

“As of today, a very strong El Niño is now present in the tropical Pacific, as of today, based on the pre-assessment of global prediction centers as well,” PAGASA Climate Monitoring and Prediction Section Chief Ana Liza Solis she said during the House Committee on Agriculture and Food hearing.

“Most climate models predict that the ongoing El Niño will persist until the first quarter of 2027, with its peak expected before the end of 2026. And its associated impacts may continue through the first half of 2027,” she added.
According to PAGASA’s climate outlook, the prolonged dry spell will lead to drought, and there will be warmer surface temperatures nationwide.
However, PAGASA said tropical cyclones and heavy rainfall may still occur.
Per the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) 356,800 Filipinos have already been affected by the El Niño in October.

Meanwhile, according to a September 2027 report by US-based Climate Impact Lab, half a million people around the world are at risk of heat-related deaths because of the phenomenon. In the Philippines, there could be more or less 6,500 heat-related deaths until February 2027.

As the Department of Environment and Natural Resources prepares water structures, rainwater harvesting systems for El Niño, the Department of Agriculture said agri damage due to El Niño has already topped P8.57B in October. — LA, GMA News

articles.title: A year after Tino: Cebu survivors strive to reclaim all they lost
articles.summary: Gina Paumba didn’t just lose her house in the aftermath of Typhoon Tino, she lost 7 years of happy memories and what she would have been her grandchildren's inheritance

items: Gina Paumba, a resident of Talisay City, lost her home and over 20 years of her family's life due to Typhoon Tino, which caused significant flooding and destruction in Cebu.

The provincial government is working on recovery efforts, including rebuilding infrastructure and providing financial assistance to affected families, but challenges remain in housing displaced residents.
On the first anniversary of the disaster, survivors commemorated the event with a protest highlighting ongoing issues of government neglect and the need for justice for the victims.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
CEBU, Philippines – Talisay City resident Gina Paumba wakes up every morning to a reminder of all that Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) took from her.
More than 20 years of her life on land her family owned, including 7 years of building a home she would have passed down to her grandchildren, were lost overnight on November 4, 2025.
“Gikan sa 2005 katong naabot mi diri, kato pa ko kasugat og tubig nga gikan didto abot dinha. Mao to ang pinakakuyaw nga baha nga among nasaksi,” Paumba told Rappler on Tuesday, November 3.
(Since we arrived here in 2005, that was the only time we saw the water reach here and there. That was the most dangerous flood we’ve ever witnessed.)
As early as the afternoon of November 3, 2025, Paumba’s family, along with their neighbors in Sitio Bogo, Camp 4, Talisay City, were already advised to head for evacuation centers.
Paumba’s home was located on the edge of the sitio along the upper part of the Mananga River. When the river began to swell, they were the first in their neighborhood to know.

Her family didn’t sleep on the eve of November 3—not because the howling winds made the shanties in their neighborhood collapse one after the other—but because all their belongings would be gone if they hadn’t kept watch of their house.
They had not yet retreated to the Camp 4 Elementary School. It was only when the ground below their house finally caved in that they evacuated.
“Nagdako akong mga anak ana dihang balaya (My children grew up in that house),” Paumba shared.

blocks.caption: WHAT’S LEFT. Gina Paumba looks at the ruins of her old home found near the Mananga River in Talisay City, Cebu, on November 3, 2026.

blocks.text: She and her family now live in a makeshift house, built from a mixture of scrap materials and other supplies provided through government assistance and donations.
They were able to get housing aid worth P10,000 from the National Housing Authority, P8,000 cash aid from the Talisay City government, and a P5,000 donation from a private foundation.

Paumba said she was very thankful for the help yet could not help but be bothered by how much Tino’s damage cost their family. For a family of 10 who work primarily as rag makers earning P12 per rag, what they make now will never be enough to cover what they lost, Paumba lamented.
The Paumbas are only one out of 157,000 families in Cebu who lost their homes to the floods caused by Tino’s downpour.
Data from the Cebu provincial government show that the typhoon left 143 fatalities with 45 people counted as missing. Around 160,000 houses, 22 bridges, and 28 roads were damaged.
Cebu Provincial Planning and Development Officer Elizar Sabinay Jr. told Rappler in an interview that the province has gradually recovered, specifically on rebuilding public infrastructures.
“We’re diverting our attention now to supporting infrastructures such as roads. It’s where the province has direct control,” Sabinay said.

Schools, according to the planning officer, are among the top priorities for rebuilding because the school buildings also serve as evacuation centers. Data from the Department of Education show that at least 1,022 schools were damaged by Tino.
Sabinay shared that the province is looking into developing existing schools into “smart classrooms” that utilize solar-powered systems and have their own water catchment infrastructure.

The recurring challenge, Sabinay stressed, is how the province will house the remaining displaced residents. Multiple considerations like the recovery of flood plains and river easements, urban congestion and distance/access to social services limit where local governments can establish new resettlements, he said.

blocks.caption: STILL REBUILDING. A year after Typhoon Tino, residents in Barangay Cotcot, Liloan, postpone civil works for a solemn Mass commemorating the first anniversary of the disaster, on November 4, 2026

blocks.text: “The province’s role now is to secure the commitments from the national department secretaries… the whole cost of the damage is [massive] but the release of funding is still [only] 10% from the commitments,” the planning officer said.
For a full recovery, the province would need at least P11 billion for roads and bridges, slope protection structures, health centers and schools.

According to the Cebu Provincial Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (PDRRMO), the province has provided around P21.98 million worth of food and non-food items to affected communities, and allocated P142.25 million for financial assistance for more than 14,000 displaced families.
At present, the provincial government is funneling P206.6 million for infrastructure projects in heavily affected areas in the towns of Compostela and Balamban, which reported a high casualty count.

Reflecting on the pain brought by the typhoon, families in Cebu commemorated the first anniversary of the disaster with an early morning penitential walk in the neighboring towns of Liloan and Compostela.

The quiet celebration was followed by a 10 am protest in in front of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Cebu City District Engineering Office, where activists and bereaved families placed small wooden crosses symbolizing lives lost over alleged government neglect and corruption.

“Wala gihapon makab-ot ang hustisya para sa mga biktima sa Bagyong Tino (Justice has not yet been delivered for the victims of Typhoon Tino),” Jaime Paglinawan, coordinator of BAYAN Central Visayas, told reporters during the protest.

blocks.caption: GRIEF. On the first anniversary of Typhoon Tino’s devastation, survivors plant small wooden crosses symbolizing lives lost over allegations of government neglect and corruption, in a protest in front of the DPWH Cebu City District Engineering Office in Cebu City on November 4, 2026.

blocks.text: Paglinawan stressed that many public officials linked to the flood control scandal still don’t have cases filed against them, while thousands of displaced families have to deal with cash assistance barely enough to compensate for what they lost to the disaster.

“What hurts most is that the poor are blamed for the floods, as if they are dumping all the garbage and living along the banks of rivers, and that they deserve to be displaced,” Paglinawan said in Cebuano.

“The real issue is being covered up, which is that our mountains are being quarried, development is taking place in the uplands, our drainage system is a failure, and the funds are being corrupted,” he added.

In the end, for Tino survivors like Paumba, recovery will be a slow and painful process—one that will probably take more years of hardships and suffering, and perhaps, more days of waking up to what she had lost.
And yet, despite all that was lost, Paumba said, she’s glad she has her family with her so she doesn’t have to do it alone. – Rappler.com
