articles.title: Home in Amherstburg, Ont., unlivable after family spent $155K on renovations, police looking for contractor
articles.summary: Tonya Azevedo says she lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe. “I’m…

image.caption: Amherstburg, Ont., resident Tonya Azevedo stands in the backyard of her Alma Street home that her family can't live in because of unsafe work done during renovations. (Jason Viau/CBC)

blocks.text: Windsor

Tonya Azevedo says she lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe. “I’m absolutely heartbroken,” says Azevedo, who had remortgaged her home to pay for the renos.
'This is just the level of destruction that we’re left with,' says Tonya Azevedo
Tonya Azevedo says she has lost $155,000 and her family of four can no longer live in their home of 20 years after a contractor who told them he was licensed did work that turned out to be unsafe.
Azevedo said she discovered dirt used to fill concrete blocks in the foundation of the home’s addition, live electrical wiring under drywall and a sewer pipe that was ruptured.
The Town of Amherstburg even ordered a stop to construction because the work didn’t match approved drawings and “multiple deficiencies” were found, according to documents obtained by CBC News.
“I’m absolutely heartbroken,” said Azevedo. “Every time I come here and see what’s left of a home that I raised my two children in and all of the happy memories … it’s just gone.”
She remortgaged her Alma Street home to get $200,000 from the bank for an addition and new garage.
There were plans to build onto the rear of the home, expand the family kitchen and the master bedroom, and add an en suite bathroom and a third bedroom upstairs.
Azevedo said she just finished spending the remainder of the loan undoing and fixing the contractor's work.
In the meantime, the family is living with a relative. Azevedo and her husband are sleeping in that home's laundry room.
“We don’t have a home,” said Azevedo. “This is just the level of destruction that we’re left with.”
Police looking to charge contractor
Windsor police said Tuesday that there's now a warrant out for the arrest of contractor Jessie Flaricee after Azevedo filed a report with Windsor police's Amherstburg detachment.
Flaricee is wanted on fraud over $5,000, uttering a forged document and obtaining more than $5,000 under false pretenses.
His company, MBS Home Solutions, was dissolved for non-compliance in November 2024, according to Windsor police.
During a conversation with CBC News on Monday, Flaricee said he offered to fix the issues, has made attempts to reach out to the family and there’s been a communication breakdown.
“They pretty much fired me and didn’t give me the opportunity to fix any issues."
Jessie Flaricee is the owner of MBS Building Solutions and did work on Azevedo's home from March to August. (Facebook)
Flaricee said he also hired subcontractors, but didn’t specify who did the problematic work.

“There is more to the story than portraying it as a contractor trying to take somebody’s money. That’s not even close to the case,” said Flaricee. “There are a lot of layers to this situation that are far more complex than what is being portrayed.”
When asked if there's any remaining money that could be returned to Azevedo, Flaricee said “that’ll be between me and her.”
“There’s no intent to take anything from anybody,” said Flaricee.
Azevedo said Flaricee told her he was a fully licensed contractor, something she says is not true.
“I guess it expired, so I had to renew it, but I’m insured. My bank account is under my business name and my name,” he said.
“People have now touched that project and started working and undoing or doing [work]."
'We trusted this person'
Azevedo said her husband knew Flaricee from the local youth football community and he quickly became a family friend.
“We trusted this person,” said Azevedo. “Maybe we shouldn’t have listened to him and had just done some more research. I was just too trusting of him.”
The Better Business Bureau (BBB) said every contractor should provide the type of licence they have, what agency it’s registered with and when it expires.

“So if you want to dig into the broader term of validating licensing, check directly with the issuing authority, which is easy to do online as well,” said Jennifer Matthews, CEO of the BBB in southwestern Ontario.
Some tips for consumer protection
Matthews said people should also ask for three references.
The BBB’s website allows the public to check the experience and reputation of companies, which Matthews also recommends doing.
“You can look at are their complaints against that business, how have they been resolved."

Demolition and construction first began in March, when she first gave Flaricee $45,000 to get started. That’s when the family packed up all of their things and moved out while the work was being done.
They moved back in by June and then the work stopped in August.
Azevedo said Flaricee asked for more money, but she refused.
She remembers telling him that she doesn’t “feel comfortable giving you any more money until there is close to $155,000 worth of work here and a home that we can live in safely.”
Tonya Azevedo, left, is seen with her husband, Joel Charron, right, her son, Bradley Azevedo and her daughter, Jocelyn Azevedo. (Tonya Azevedo)
In Azevedo's case, there was an attempt to figure out where the money went. She said she asked for invoices and receipts, and never received them.
But Flaricee insisted he was fired and not given the opportunity to fix the problems.
Son's 'safe space and sanctuary' is now gone
Either way, Azevedo said, there’s been a lot of “stress and trauma” put on her family throughout this process.
Her 16-year-old son, who has autism, just wants his bedroom back. She calls it his “safe space and sanctuary" and said it's taken a toll on his mental health.
“To have everything stripped away from them and as a mom, not being able to fix that," said Azevedo.
The town’s building department noted that the foundation mortar joints didn’t comply with the Ontario Building Code and new part of the foundation was not connected to the existing foundation.
After the contractor’s demolition, Azevedo said, there’s been no heat in the home, the family is without a washroom and there isn’t power to much of the house.
“We’re not asking for our home to be finished. We’re just asking for our home back."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Viau is reporter for CBC News based in Windsor, Ont. He has an interest in telling stories related to accountability, policing, court, crime and municipal affairs. You can email story ideas and tips to jason.viau@cbc.ca.

articles.title: UK's King Charles III decries 'monstrous injustice' of slave trade
articles.summary: King Charles has told leaders at a Commonwealth summit that the legacy of the transatlantic slave trade "fills my heart with horror." He did not address calls for apologies and reparations.

image.caption: King Charles III opened the 28th Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting with earnest words of reflection, though he offered no apologies for the British Empire's role in the transatlantic slave tradeImage: Ben Stansall/REUTERS

blocks.text: The United Kingdom's King Charles III on Tuesday opened this week's Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda, a summit of 56 Commonwealth member-state leaders, by speaking of the tragic legacy of the transatlantic slave trade.
Charles told those gathered that he had furthered his "own understanding of the issues through listening, learning and looking."

"The ​transatlantic trade in enslaved persons still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth. As I have said before, that shameful chapter of history is one that fills my heart with ⁠horror ​and my soul with the most profound personal sorrow."

The monarch stopped short of apologizing for Britain's role in the dark trade, as well as refraining from any talk of reparations. Instead, he spoke of the need to look forward when addressing the "monstrous injustice" of the past to insure that "evil need not have the last word."
Ghana revives slave trade history through theater
Will the UK apologize for slavery, offer reparations?

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who is also in attendance, has previously said that he could be open to an apology, and the run up to the summit has been dominated by talk of apologies and potential financial reparations.

Both the king and the prime minister have spoken of using the summit as an opportunity to address future partnerships by devising approaches to tackle healthcare, education and climate protection needs among those "who struggle against ⁠hardship and disadvantage" rather than dwelling on the past.
"We cannot change the actions of those who came before us," said the monarch as he opened Tuesday's session, "We can, however, learn from the past."

Burnham has said he would like to discuss debt resets for smaller Commonwealth nations as well as announcing ⁠a €48.2 million ($54 million) investment into ​critical infrastructure in the Caribbean over the next three years.

blocks.caption: Despite calls for reparations, King Charles has emphasized building strong future partnerships within the Commonwealth rather than dwelling on the pastImage: Matias Delacroix/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What was the British Empire's role in the transatlantic slave trade?

The British joined the institutionalized slave trade in the seventeenth century, and quickly eclipsed other European powers before involvement in the trade was outlawed for British subjects in the Slave Trade Act of 1807 and then done away with in the wider British Empire in the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833.

During that time, Britain outfitted almost one-third of all transatlantic slave voyages, facilitating the forced transport of over 3.2 million Africans, mainly to British colonies in the Caribbean and North America.
The Commonwealth of Nations consists largely of former British colonies whose combined GDP of roughly $14.5 trillion accounts for about 15% of the global economy.
The Commonwealth in Africa: Real impact or empty promises?

articles.title: Seven flights across Europe targeted by suspected bomb threats
articles.summary: Planes in Poland, Spain, Bulgaria and Italy have been checked for explosives following separate threats.
articles.byline: Emer Moreau, Jaroslav Lukiv, Laura Gozzi

blocks.text: Seven passenger planes across Europe, two of which departed from the UK, have been inspected following a series of suspected bomb threats.

Two Ryanair flights, one originating from Dublin and the other from Lisbon, were searched after landing in Rome following anonymous tips but no explosives were found, sources at the city's Fiumicino airport told the BBC.
The Dublin flight was escorted by the Italian Air Force until landing. Authorities have also searched planes in Poland, Spain and Bulgaria.
While officially there is no link between them, authorities from various countries will be co-operating to assess whether this was a co-ordinated attack, designed to disrupt airspace.
The UK government described today's incidents as "malicious hoax threats".

In a statement it said it had "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world, with well-tested processes for dealing with any potential threats, as well as malicious hoax threats, like those we've seen today".
Aviation security expert Paul Mason said bomb threats on passenger planes "don't happen that frequently", which made the latest incidents "unusual".

"It sounds like they've been made in a credible manner across a broad range of airlines," Mason told BBC Radio 5 Live. "That would suggest to me that it's been a very deliberate act by a typical actor rather than a load of coincidental, malicious calls."
He said "there are a lot of processes" that the onboard crew and people on the ground must go through "to validate the credibility of the threat".

A flight may be asked to divert if the credibility of a threat "is of a certain level", Mason added, and in some cases the onboard crew may not even be advised on what the ground operators were dealing with.
In Rome, sources at Fiumicino airport told the BBC police bomb disposal experts carried out standard security protocols to ensure the safety of all passengers and crew.
Inspections of the passengers, luggage, and the aircraft yielded negative results, and the alert has since been cleared.
One plane which landed in Murcia, southern Spain - a Ryanair flight coming from Manchester - was also found not to have any explosives on board, Spanish authorities said.
One passenger later said she was unaware of the bomb threat until after the plane landed.
"We weren't told anything during the flight," Sarah told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The plane stopped quite suddenly and then we were kept on the runway for around 30 minutes."
"Then the fire engines turned up, the bomb squad turned up and we were asked to evacuate," she continues.

Sarah said the plane had not been on the ground a minute before it was "surrounded by fire engines and police and a bomb squad". All the passengers were then escorted by police, leaving all their belongings.
"We were only later told that it was an actual threat, a bomb threat to the plane itself," she added.
Two flights heading to Warsaw were also affected, including one from London Heathrow.
The Heathrow flight was originally meant to land at the Polish capital's main airport, Chopin, but was diverted instead to the smaller Modlin airport, briefly forcing its closure.
A Scandinavian Airlines flight from Copenhagen to Warsaw-Chopin landed as planned.
Later on Tuesday, Bulgarian Transport Minister Georgi Peev said there were bomb threats against two planes travelling to the country's capital Sofia.
He told the state-owned Bulgarian News Agency (BTA) the flights were from the northern Italian city of Bergamo and Ireland's capital Dublin.
The flights into Sofia were not diverted and no explosives were found when the planes were checked, Peev said.

Bulgaria's border police said in a statement sent to the BBC that at around 10:35 (08:35 GMT) it had received an email about "the presence of an improvised explosive device on a flight returning from Bergamo".
"Standard procedures for such incidents were immediately activated, and an operational headquarters comprising representatives of various institutions was convened," the statement said.
The border police added that the same email also reported a "similar threat against aircraft arriving from Dublin".
These incidents come a day after a Wizz Air flight from London Luton made an emergency landing in Budapest, escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet, after a bomb threat.
Wizz Air said later that security checks had been made and nothing was found.
BBC Verify has consulted aviation safety experts about what happens on board a plane when a bomb threat is issued.

Marco Chan, a former pilot for Cathay Pacific Airways and Hong Kong Airlines who is now a senior lecturer in aviation operations at Kingston University, said a bomb threat is considered "genuine until it is resolved, even though most turn out to be hoaxes".

Chan said crews will "quietly search" toilets, galleys and storage areas and will not touch a suspicious item unless it has to be taken to an area on the aircraft designated as the least risky bomb location.
The aircraft's captain will have multiple factors to assess, according to former airline pilot Terry Tozer, an aviation safety commentator.
He said these include what facilities are available at the airport they are being diverted to and how the plane can continue onwards should it turn out to be a false threat.
Chan added that once on the ground, the plane is generally "taken to an isolated stand, passengers are disembarked, and police and bomb disposal teams search it".

articles.title: The transplanted Scot doing famous father proud in New Zealand
articles.summary: Clark Laidlaw, head coach at Super Rugby champions Hurricanes, has made a huge impact in New Zealand and would "welcome a conversation" about taking on the top job in Scotland.

blocks.text: A few weeks back, four Scots shot the breeze in New Zealand, a meeting of rugby intellects transplanted from Edinburgh, Inverness, Yetholm and Jedburgh - all of them doing great things in their adopted land.
Mike Blair was one of them. On Saturday, in what promises to be a surreal day for him, the former Scotland captain will return to Murrayfield as attack coach for the All Blacks.
Euan Mackintosh was another. Mackintosh is the All Blacks' skills acquisition coach. The third man was Adam Hay, who is New Zealand's performance scientist.
The fourth was Clark Laidlaw, son of the great Roy, cousin of Greig and Super Rugby champion coach in 2026.
"We were getting a bit of stick at lunch, the four of us talking Scottish," says Laidlaw, whose Hurricanes team not only won Super Rugby in late June, they dominated it.

Finishing top of the table when the regular season ended, they won their first knockout game 66-12 against the Brumbies, then beat the Blues 57-21 in the semi-final before dismantling the Chiefs 60-5 in the final.
It was Laidlaw's third season in charge. He's far more celebrated in New Zealand than he is at home.

He's been there for 18 years, on and off, and he spoke about his life and times on the BBC's Scotland Rugby Podcast, how he went from a school-leaver at 16 to a New Zealand sevens coach - Commonwealth Games gold, World Cup Sevens gold, Olympics silver in Tokyo - to winning the ultimate club prize in southern hemisphere rugby in the summer.
Eight of Laidlaw's Hurricanes players are in Dave Rennie's touring squad and it might have been double figures had injury not taken a number of others out of the reckoning.
Laidlaw is a New Zealand passport holder now, but he'll be on Scotland's side on Saturday.
"You're gonna see New Zealand's strongest possible team, but there's no reason why Scotland can't win," he reckons. "It's been a bounce of the ball here and there [in recent games].
"Scotland are definitely knocking on the door. I want Scotland to beat the All Blacks and I want the All Blacks to win every other game."
He was 30 when he left Scotland for Taranaki, as a skills coach on the north island. Given his upbringing he always had a curiosity in him. His father always spoke about being a student of the game.
"I just thought there must be different ways to look at the game and different ways to look at life, really," he explains.
"I used to go and pass my rugby ball against a tree at lunchtime and train at night. I used to say to the old boys, I wasn't going to be staying here.
"They'd be like, 'Yeah, you'll be here'. I just knew I didn't want to be there for 20 years. It's not like I had a bad life in Scotland.
"I had a great job at East Lothian Council and I was coaching Jed-Forest. But I was curious to see what was outside of those big walls in Jed."

New Zealand has changed him, he says. Not just as a rugby man, but as a husband and father. The Maori and Pacific Island culture has influenced him in a substantial way, knocking some rough edges off his personality.
"Being around so many different people from different backgrounds took a little bit of my aggressive Scottish side off me," he says.
"Not too much, I hope. I have more empathy and more of an understanding side and I certainly didn't have that when I was younger."
That process started during his wildly successful years on the Sevens beat.
"The types of athletes we would bring in were often young, so it became an environment where we did have to look after each other," he says. "We had to look after young players.
"Mums and dads were sending their kids off to the Sevens. It was the first time they were leaving home. So we did have to have a caring element to that programme as well as driving them forward."
His time in New Zealand was interrupted by a brief spell at London Irish a decade ago. Around that time, he had opportunities to go to Leinster and Montpellier but he turned them down.
After two seasons, he was lured back to New Zealand - and his life really started to change.
All of this begs the question about his future. Is he a potential All Blacks head coach? Would he welcome a conversation about taking over from Gregor Townsend after the World Cup?
He thinks Kiwis are open-minded on coaches who they feel can help them win. Himself and Blair are proof of that.

The Scotland gig is more immediate, of course. "Gregor's done an amazing job," he answers. "Lots of coaches around the world will be looking at that job with real excitement for whenever Gregor moves on.
"I'd welcome a conversation. It would be a lot to up sticks and move back to Scotland, but you never know in sport.

"One thing I have learned is you can't plan. My focus is on the Hurricanes. If that leads to international rugby somewhere one day then I would definitely look at it, but looking too far ahead can trip you up."
He speaks about his dad, how proud he is of him and also of the pain of seeing him living with dementia.

In eight years as a Test player - courage and class in equal measure in the number nine jersey - Roy got 47 Scotland caps and four Lions caps. "That would be 120 games nowadays, wouldn't it," says his son.
"How is he? The short answer is he's doing as good as he can. He's safe and healthy. He's in a care home in Jed and is well looked after.
"The family is amazing. Greig's mum and dad are amazing. My middle brother lives close by and I feel for him because it's tough on him.
"John Rutherford and Keith Robertson [his fellow 1984 Grand Slam winners] go across every week and sit with him. It's one of the hardest things about being on this side of the world.
"It's always in the back of your head that Scotland is home and moving back at some stage might be an option."
Deep down, you hope Roy knows the heights his son has reached in the game and what a massive part he played in it all.
It's been some journey so far - and you sense there are many more adventures to come, at home or in his home from home.

articles.title: Trump says US will end military aid to Israel by the end of this year
articles.summary:
US president makes surprise election day announcement, saying country does not ‘need’ $4bn annual payment

Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this…

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said that the US will end military aid to Israel at the end of this year in a surprise election day announcement that appeared to be targeted at voters sceptical of US support for Israel and the war in Gaza.
In a phone interview with Fox News as voting began on Tuesday morning, Trump said the US would cut nearly $4bn (£2.96bn) in military aid to Israel because “they don’t need it.”
“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.

Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed, pictured campaigning on Monday, would become the US’s first Muslim senator if elected. Photograph: Zach D Roberts/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.

Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as Foreign Military Financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.

Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, where US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. He would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.
after newsletter promotion

A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.

Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president JD Vance has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”

During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

articles.title: Binance says fake job interviews used as part of $6.3bn crypto hack
articles.summary: An engineer was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives, Binance says.

blocks.text: Hackers who stole a record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) from Binance used fake job interviews and a compromised internal AI tool, the firm has revealed.
Initial findings published by the company, which operates the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said hackers gained access to its systems through "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign".

It said they used a range of techniques such as malicious software downloads to compromise the computers of Binance engineers and gain control over tools to drain its wallet of billions of dollars worth of crypto.
Binance called it a "serious and highly sophisticated security incident" and apologised, saying "this should not have happened".
In a post on X, external, Binance said hackers targeted its engineers using social engineering techniques.
These see hackers use approaches such as phishing to trick people into parting with sensitive or personal details, that can then be used to try and access their accounts.
Binance said as part of the hack, one of its engineers was contacted through a legitimate job-hunting platform and invited to bogus job interviews with fake company representatives.
It said the perpetrators used "more advanced and deceptive" methods to build trust with him, such as sharing social media accounts that contained personal images.
The engineer in question was instructed to download malware masquerading as an "assignment" during a second interview, that deployed malicious code with "obfuscation techniques" evading detection.

Binance said hackers then leveraged the engineer's compromised computer and a compromised internal AI tool in October to gain control over two other engineers' laptops, and execute the next steps of the attack.
The incident led Binance to suspend withdrawals for customers globally, meaning users could not get their cryptocurrency out of the platform until the service was restored on Sunday.
Customers withdrew billions of dollars worth of assets after it reopened.
"We apologise for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry," it said.
The company added it had taken a range of steps following the incident, including working with law enforcement to trace and freeze affected assets.
It said it had also set aside more than 100% of the funds needed to cover the loss, noting 98% of the token assets impacted had been "replenished" as of Saturday.
The record $6.3bn (£4.7bn) attack is thought to be the largest crypto hack to date.
US crime agencies, including the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Secret Service, have been assisting Binance in tracing the crypto taken from the platform's own wallets.
The agencies, along with a range of cyber analysts, said that the hack - like similar breaches before it - bore the signs of having been orchestrated by North Korea.
Pyongyang hit back at the claims on Tuesday, denying it was behind the hack.

Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on the accusations were another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage North Korea's public image.
The country has consistently denied being behind a number of major cyber attacks it has been blamed for in recent years.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Binance had previously not responded to the BBC's queries about North Korea's alleged involvement in the hack.

But on Tuesday, the company wrote in its post on X, external: "The latest information released by the Federal Bureau of Investigation indicates that the Democratic People's Republic of Korea is responsible for this incident."

As part of its security efforts following the attack, Binance said it would also increase investment in AI tools that can detect security threats, as well as engage third-party cyber experts to carry out a full-scale review of the incident.
It also said that it would seek to stablish a security research fund and work with leading AI and security firms on targeted initiatives.

articles.title: How sporting events are being impacted by Middle East conflict
articles.summary: BBC Sport takes a look at how the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has affected sporting events in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain and the wider area.

blocks.text: The Saudi Pro League has, for the most part, managed to carry on as usual.
Several ​domestic ⁠league games had to be postponed, including three fixtures last month as the situation escalated.

The games were moved in the immediate aftermath of the attack on a major airport in Riyadh - though the SPL said they were switched "as a result of mandatory minimum rest periods between matches and to accommodate logistical requirements".
Following the postponement of the Asian Cup, this weekend's full round of Saudi Pro League has been called off.

The league once again has not attributed this to conflict in the region, instead saying the calendar would be recalibrated after the cancellation of the Asian Cup to achieve "a more balanced distribution of fixtures".
The AFC Champions League has been affected as well.
Cristiano Ronaldo and Kingsley Coman were among Al-Nassr's star players who did not to fly to Uzbekistan this week "given the pressure of matches and the amount of travel involved".
Al-Wasl of the United Arab Emirates also opted not to fly to Saudi Arabia to play Al-Nassr, and the match will be rearranged.
Meanwhile, the wife of Ollie Watkins, who plays for Riyadh-based Al-Hilal, posted on TikTok that she would be staying in the UK with their two children "until it calms down".
"We've had a bit of a plot twist," said Ellie Watkins. "I have come back to the UK for a little bit.
"There's just a little bit of conflict and things going on over in Saudi and we basically decided just to stay here.
"I felt like I needed to do that for the kids so there is some form of normality until we can get back out there and all be together."
Other well-known stars playing in the country include Gabriel Martinelli, Tijjani Reijnders, Darwin Nunez, Ivan Toney, Alexandre Lacazette, Ruben Neves, Sadio Mane and Joao Felix.
Andrew Benson, F1 Correspondent
Formula 1 has a major dilemma about racing in the Middle East both at the end of this season and the beginning of next.
Most pressingly, the 2026 season is due to end with races in Qatar on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.
As things stand, the sport is pressing ahead with plans to go to those races after being given security reassurances from various governmental sources that it should be safe.
There are, though, many people within the sport with misgivings about going.
Should the situation in the Middle East deteriorate in the next week or so, they could be called off and replaced with a single event in Imola in Italy on the Abu Dhabi weekend.
The 2027 season is scheduled to start in Bahrain on 12-14 March, with Saudi Arabia hosting on the following weekend.
But as things stand between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthi separatists, that race could not go ahead, and is likely to be cancelled if nothing changes by December.

Bahrain and Saudi Arabia are linked by a causeway, at the Saudi end of which is a facility belonging to state oil company Aramco, which has been targeted by the Houthis, while it joins Bahrain close to the F1 track.
So Bahrain is also be in jeopardy.
One option being discussed is to hold that race in Malaysia, as was done in October this year.
The Six Kings Slam, which should have begun on Saturday in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, has been postponed by two months.

It is now scheduled to run from 27 December to 30 December at the ANB Arena, located about 31km away from the King Khalid International Airport, which was the target of an attack on 10 October that killed 13 people and injured 308 others.
Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Alex de Minaur, Taylor Fritz and Learner Tien are due to compete.
But the 2026 WTA Finals, this weekend's season-ending championship of the women's tour, will not take place in Saudi Arabia.
A mutual agreement was reached to terminate a hosting agreement early, and it will instead take place at Indian Wells in the United States.
The FIFAe Finals, an esports tournament series organised by Fifa, should have taken place in Jeddah last month but was cancelled.

This week's UCI Urban Cycling World Championships, for the world's leading riders in trials and BMX Freestyle, in Riyadh was called off too, with a decision due "on the sporting consequences of this announcement".
The PIF Saudi International event, the season finale of the Asian Tour, will not be held between 18-21 November at Riyadh Golf Club.
After "an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament" the decision was taken to call it off.
And on Tuesday, the Professional Triathletes Organisation said it was moving the Saudi Arabia T100 and World Triathlon Cup, in Jeddah, from the end of this month to 16-17 April.

articles.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’
articles.summary: A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final…

blocks.text: It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.

As Nobel laureate economist Amartya Sen once wrote, Tagore was “a towering figure in the millennium-old literature of Bengal”, whose songs resonate across eastern India and Bangladesh, while his ideas on education, nationalism and freedom of the mind remain relevant today.

Yet his work also made a deep impression on the literary world far beyond the shores of India. WB Yeats is said to have described Tagore as “greater than any of us”. Gitanjali, the collection of poems that won Tagore the Nobel prize that same year, was praised by the committee for its “profoundly sensitive, fresh and beautiful verse”. Tagore’s English translation was published in London that March and reprinted 10 times by the time the prize was announced in November.

Tagore’s life and works have, of course, been well documented, but a collection of material preserved in a private family archive is now being brought into public view for the first time at an exhibition by Christie’s, opening in Mumbai this month. The archive draws from Tagore’s visits to the family home of his protege, Maitreyi Devi, in the bucolic village of Mungpoo in Darjeeling between 1938 and 1940. He died in 1941.

blocks.caption: An intimate glimpse … one of Tagore’s unseen artwork on display. Photograph: Christie’s Images Ltd 2026

blocks.text: The collection on display – artworks, manuscripts, letters, photographs and personal effects – offers an intimate glimpse into Tagore’s creative process and personal world in his final years.
I spoke to the exhibition curator, Nishad Avari, head of south Asian modern and contemporary art at Christie’s, about the stories behind the archive.

One instructive document Avari points to is a manuscript from 1940. It appears to be a draft of Tagore’s memoir Chelebela or My Boyhood Days, in which he reflects on his life – from growing up in a large family in Calcutta (modern-day Kolkata) to the rapidly changing world ushered in by electricity and the motorcar.

For Avari, what stood out was how the ideas in the document echoed the educational philosophy Tagore put into practice in Santiniketan (or Abode of Peace), the experimental school he set up about 100 miles from the state capital.
“He speaks about how education is like being in prison and that it should be open and free … about the idea of wonder and even fear as inspiring creativity,” Avari told me.

“That’s a direct relationship to Santiniketan and the open model of the school where people sat under trees with their gurus and learned in the open. Education didn’t feel like a restriction, prison or imposition,” he added.

blocks.caption: Window to a master’s practice … A manuscript by Rabindranath Tagore, on display at Christie’s. Photograph: Christie’s Images Ltd 2026

blocks.text: Avari points to another detail that makes this particular document valuable. Of the 10 complete manuscripts in the exhibition, it is the only one dictated to Devi, whose father was a close friend of Tagore’s. For Avari, this speaks to their close relationship and the trust he placed in her.

“If you look at the collection as a whole, she has copies of almost every single one of his publications signed to her by him,” he says. The collection includes hundreds of letters, too: first between Tagore and her father, and later between Tagore and Devi herself.

There are doodles among corrections, Avari explains, which show how his literary practice fed into his artistic practice. Alongside the manuscripts and correspondence are vintage photographs and personal effects, including a kurta and a lungi that Tagore left behind at the family home.

Among the artworks in the collection is a portrait of Devi, particularly notable because Tagore’s figure studies were not generally attributed to specific individuals in the way that portraits by his nephews, Abanindranath and Gaganendranath, often were, Avari said. There is also a landscape depicting the forests of Mungpoo, which Tagore embraced as a retreat.
On the international art market, Tagore’s paintings command significant prices. This year, Sotheby’s sold one of his watercolours for £1.02m (Rs 12.97 crore), nearly four times its low estimate.
Institutions such as Visva-Bharati in Santiniketan and the National Gallery of Modern Art hold much of Tagore’s archival materials, making the discovery of a private archive particularly rare.

He hopes that making these materials public will offer historians, scholars and admirers alike additional perspectives on Tagore. “We hope to add to the understanding of the artist, their career, and in this case, of course, our understanding of the man beyond his art as well.”
Rabindranath Tagore and Mungpoo runs between 10 November and 18 December at Christie’s space in south Mumbai.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: Ready for talk? … India’s defence minister, Rajnath Singh, at a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in Tajikistan in October.  Photograph: Alexander Miridonov/Sputnik/Government Press Service/EPA

blocks.text: Politics | India has invited Pakistan to attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation’s Civilisational Dialogue Forum in New Delhi later this month, the Indian Express reported. It is the first invitation since the two neighbouring states engaged in a military conflict last year.

Law | Twenty-one media organisations have challenged India’s privacy laws in court, arguing that the controversial provisions threaten press freedom, Reuters reported. The petition warns that the law could expose journalists’ sources and force publishers to remove stories at the direction of authorities.
after newsletter promotion

Academia | Indian academic Mahmood Kooria, a lecturer at the University of Edinburgh, is among this year’s recipients of the Philip Leverhulme prize in Humanities. The £100,000 award recognises his work on the premodern Indian Ocean world.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: A voyage through another time … Malvika Singh’s Cooking for my Firefly. Photograph: Handout

blocks.text: Freddy Birdy, a copywriter whose delightful words have earned him a devoted Instagram following, recommends writer and historian Malvika Singh’s cookbook, Cooking for My Firefly.

“This book isn’t about recipes, though it does include them. It is a voyage through another time and place, tracing the social fabric of India of the 60s, 70s and 80s, trickling down to today. Told in Malvika’s beautiful prose, it takes us to a time when people entertained in homes, not in restaurants; when dishes were cooked in-house and there were no caterers or party planners. An era long before Instagram posts, WhatsApp invitations, celebrity chefs and food delivery apps, when the point of having a party was simply to have fun. It is an archive of photographs, food, culture, gossip, movie stars, politicians, royalty, set against the spectacular backdrop of Malvika’s dining tables through the decades. I like to dip into it every now and then, much as one might do standing in a dark kitchen with the light of the refrigerator enticing you to midnight goodies.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: Sharp rise since 2023 … The Times of India reports that Indians lost Rs 22,495 crore (£1.77bn) to cyberfraud in 2025. Photograph: Tim Goode/PA

blocks.text: Indians lost Rs 22,495 crore (£1.77bn) to cyberfraud in 2025, Times of India reported citing data from the Home Ministry. While the figure is marginally down from the previous year, losses have risen sharply since 2023.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: ‘We’ll find a way to sing’ … Dopeher Blues by Aamir Aziz. Photograph: Youtube

blocks.text: At a time when public anger has spilled into the streets, artist Aamir Aziz’s new track, Dopeher Blues (Afternoon Blues), captures the frustration and angst of a generation that has lived through many crises.

Aziz describes the song as an expression of a period of deep suffocation. Issues such as farmer suicides, unemployment and conflicts in Palestine and Kashmir, he told me, are things he has grown up with even as public attention shifts with the news cycle. It is also a warning, in part, against internet culture, where injustices risk becoming normalised.

Aziz, 35, works in acting, music and writing, and became an internet sensation with his defiant poem Sab Yaad Rakha Jayega (Everything Will Be Remembered) during the citizenship protests. At the heart of his new track is a note of defiance and hope: “We’ll find a way to sing,” he says, as he calls on everyone “to keep speaking up even in a climate of fear, misinformation and oppression.”
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Why South Africa's local elections matter
articles.summary: South Africans head to the polls on Wednesday amid water shortages, frustration with local services and questions over whether the ANC's support will keep falling.

image.caption: Water shortages ‌and unreliable electricity ⁠supplies ⁠have become symbols of municipal failures that have angered votersImage: Themba Hadebe/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "We've decided not to vote. At all," said Vatiswa Zoya, two days before voters in South Africa cast their ballots for new municipal government leaders. "What is the point? We will still sleep hungry."
These very same frustrations are what will lead 22-year-old Lindokuhle Mbandazayo to the polls, although she has yet to decide where to place her cross.

"When we vote for councilors, we ask them to fix the area," Mbandazayo told DW. "The electricity goes off regularly here. There is also sewage in the streets and we have to jump over this. There are a lot of things that need to be fixed here."

Both women live in Tembisa, a township in Ekurhuleni, a municipality on the outskirts of Johannesburg, South Africa's largest city. Both express an "embedded frustration" over their living conditions.

blocks.caption: Many voters will be asking whether they'll have water to shower on election day, as shortages persistImage: Siphiwe Sibeko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, noted that it is this "embedded frustration" that prompts people to vote.
"Your vote actually puts some of these political parties' feet to the fire, but I think that frustration is also inherently coming from the fact that it's not going to happen overnight," Naidu said.

On Wednesday, South Africans will vote in local government elections that will determine control of the country's largest cities and test whether the African National Congress (ANC), the leading party in a national government coalition, continues its electoral decline.
Here are five things to know about the November 4 election.
1. Water as a key voter issue
Many voters will be motivated by whether they can shower or not on voting day, as many parts of the country experience water supply issues.
In Johannesburg, several neighborhoods have faced water cuts and rationing for weeks as old infrastructure struggles to keep up with supply.

"Every province has an issue. So if we take for example drinking water quality, half of the drinking water systems in South Africa are not fit for drinking," said Ferrial Adam, executive director of water rights NGO WaterCAN.

"Almost 70% of our wastewater treatment works are in a critical state and spewing sewage into rivers and streams across the country," she told DW during a protest over water cuts in Johannesburg, adding that "it is a definite water crisis across South Africa."
In Tshwane, a metropolitan area that includes South Africa's administrative capital, Pretoria, a recent water treatment failure left more than 400 residents sick.

Sanusha Naidu, an analyst at the Institute for Global Dialogue, says that despite widespread worries about water quality and supply, many of those campaigning have not provided adequate details on their solutions.

"I think their promises have been very transactional. Their promises are always, you know, we're going to bring water to your community. We're going to make sure the taps are flowing. We're going to ensure that we're going to deal with the old infrastructure around water, etc. But I don't think they've dug deeper in terms of understanding what the budgets say about water access," she said.
2. ANC in decline
Many voters place blame for the state of municipalities on the African National Congress, which has historically held an outright majority in most municipalities.

In 2016 the ANC secured 53.91% of the overall vote and had an outright majority in 161 of 213 councils. In 2021, that decreased to 45.59% of the overall vote with a majority in 122 of 213 municipalities.
Global marketing research firm Ipsos predicts that the party's support could fall as low as 30% in this election, resulting in an increase in coalition-run municipalities.
South Africa sees nationwide protests over migrants
Naidu notes that the party has struggled to keep up with the expectations of evolving voters, particularly millennial and Gen Zvoters who now make up the bulk of voters.
"You have an electorate that wants to see who are these people that you're putting out there to say you're going to make things work for us," she said.
Mbandazayo is one such voter, who is casting her ballot in her second election and says she is looking for a new voice in politics.
"We need change. I am considering voting for another party because the current party is not doing well for us because we've been voting for them for a long time," she told DW.
3. Migration a big talking point
South Africa has seen a wave of protests around migration for several months, ramping up in October with opposition to the country's asylum process.
Murmur Intelligence, a digital analysis firm, says parties including Action SA, the MK Party and the Patriotic Alliance have used immigration as a campaign issue.
"The party that might claim the most benefit from that sentiment … is Action SA, noted Murmur Intelligence co-founder Aldu Cornelissen.

"They would make a clear argument that we need to get rid of illegal immigrants. We need to improve immigration. We need to protect our borders, which are all legitimate concerns, right? So, if any of the parties could capitalize on this sentiment, it would be them."
"But for what percentage? I would wager between 6% and 8%, roughly," Cornelissen added.
Those margins may seem low, but in an increasingly fractured political landscape parties are fighting for every vote.

The Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) has said 136,760 candidates are contesting across the country, with 75 parties contesting in Johannesburg, 70 in Tshwane and 69 in eThekwini (Durban and surrounding areas).
4. Election misinformation

Fake news and false AI-generated content have become a feature in this election, with the IEC investigating over 700 complaints of disinformation. One of the prominent claims has been an accusation that the ANC plans to mobilize asylum seekers to vote for them.
Asylum seekers, refugees and permanent residents can't legally vote in South African elections regardless of how long they've been in the country.
South Africa election hit by disinformation surge

William Bird, director of media monitoring agency Moxii Africa, says misinformation and disinformation "are now kind of part and parcel of your standard build-up to any electoral environment, wherever you are in the world."

"What we see with disinformation is that it always picks up on whatever the hot button news issues are, as well as the standard kind of tropes about elections, he said, adding that there's always going to be "some bunch of clowns" saying the elections are rigged.

"And in South Africa's case, there's no evidence to support that at all. The IEC [Electoral Commission of South Africa] is one of the best electoral management bodies in the world. So of course, you then see people that are either wanting to destabilize, or they're wanting to just shake things up and make people scared or angry, and so they use those kinds of narratives. And that, unfortunately, is becoming an increasingly common trait," Bird told DW.
Bird added that social media platforms often "incentivize and deliberately encourage people" to attack others online.
5. Will people make it to the polls?

Local government election turnout has historically been lower than turnout in national elections. In 2016, turnout was at 57.95% and dropped to 45.87%. In 2024, in the most recent national elections, turnout was at 58.64%.
Naidu says this election will ultimately depend less on online discussions or campaign slogans and more on how many people make it to the polls.
Voters will mark two ballots — one for a direct local representative and a second for a political party under a proportional representation (PR) system.
Seats allocated through the PR vote account for half of all council seats, making them as important as the direct votes for councilors and this is where voter turnout becomes a key element.

"That is why political parties are saying to people, go out and vote, go out and vote, because if you don't go out and vote, it has an impact on the calculation of what you win as a PR vote in the council and the seats that you get," she said. In turn, this affects the make-up of each municipality and whether new coalition governments will form.
Could you still afford to live in Cape Town today?
Additional reporting by Ahmed Kajee and Sofia Christensen

articles.title: Ukraine war: Merz doubts Russia is serious about a truce
articles.summary: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz met with Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin, and emphasized Europe needs to be included in any peace talks with Russia. At the same time, Merz doubts Moscow is serious…

image.caption: Zelenskyy arrived hours after Russian strikes hit Ukraine, with air defense and energy support key themes in his talks with MerzImage: Markus Schreiber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Tuesday he had seen no sign that Russia was serious about negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine, speaking alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Berlin.
Both leaders said Europe must help shape any lasting peace.
Germany expects European representatives to be in Abu Dhabi for next week's US-led talks with Ukraine and Russia, though they are unlikely to have a seat at the table.

"It is important that Russia finally and seriously engages in negotiations about a ceasefire and a subsequent peace agreement," Merz said when asked about the Abu Dhabi talks. "I do not see that happening so far."

Zelenskyy said he hopes the Abu Dhabi talks, the first trilateral sit down since February, could pave the way for a direct meeting between the Ukrainian president and Russia's Vladimir Putin, who has thus far refused several offers from Zelenskyy for face-to-face talks.
"We are counting on the fact that work in this format and our other diplomatic steps will open the way to a trilateral format at the level of leaders," he told reporters.
Europe must have a say on postwar security
Merz said Europe must have a say on sanctions and postwar security.

He said the local ceasefire in Oleshky could serve as a model for a wider truce, but warned that Russian attacks in the Black Sea risked further escalation. "Russia is precipitating a global food crisis, to the detriment of the poorest nations and countries in the world," he said.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine wanted a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, safe passage for grain shipments through the Black Sea and further prisoner exchanges.
Lavrov sets conditions for talks with Zelenskyy at G20 meeting

The Ukrainian president said a ceasefire alone would not secure a lasting peace. Ukraine would need security guarantees backed by Europe and the US. He insisted Europe must be involved in the negotiations.
"There cannot be a sustainable peace if Europe is not at the negotiating table," Zelenskyy said.
He said Ukraine would join the US, European partners and NATO for talks on security guarantees and reconstruction in Brussels on Wednesday.
Russia increases attacks on Ukrainian civilians
The talks in Berlin come as Russia continues to increase airstrikes on Ukrainian civilians.

Zelenskyy said at least 33 people were killed, and more than 50 could be trapped in rubble, after multiple Russian strikes on a school building used as an aid distribution center in the frontline southeastern village of on Monday.

Ukrainian officials said Russian forces launched an initial strike on residents waiting to receive aid, and then hit the same location again after waiting for rescue personnel to arrive on the scene, killing several of them and destroying emergency vehicles.
Speaking in Berlin, Zelenskyy described the strike as "one of the largest Russian killings of this war."
On Tuesday, at least 73 people were injured in a strike on a hospital in the northeastern city of Kharkiv, and 226 patients had to be transferred to other hospitals, regional prosecutors said.

blocks.caption: Russian forces struck the aid center twice after waiting for rescue workers to arriveImage: REUTERS

blocks.text: Germany pledges aid ahead of winter
"Ahead of the next winter, air defense and the energy sector are our priorities," Merz said. He said Germany would soon deliver new aid in both areas and provide further winter assistance this year.
Zelenskyy thanked Germany for helping protect Ukraine's skies and supporting its energy infrastructure.
"Without Germany, we would not be as strong as we are," he said.
He said Ukraine urgently needed more air defense equipment, including Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy told EU leaders in October that Ukraine would need an additional €70 billion ($78 billion) from European governments next year. Germany plans to host a summit of countries backing Ukraine in mid-November to discuss further support ahead of winter.
How has Berlin stepped up security?
The visit coincides with the opening of the two-day Berlin Security Conference, which brings together European officials and defense experts. Russia's war in Ukraine is high on the agenda.
Police said about 3,400 additional officers were deployed for the visit and the conference, with reinforcements from across Germany.

Armed officers guarded barriers around parts of the government district, and special police units deployed snipers. Roads were also closed in western Berlin, including near the Kurfürstendamm shopping avenue.
Ukraine: How dachas offer refuge from war

articles.title: China and India achieved diplomatic thaw. Now the border is flaring up
articles.summary: Indian authorities have confirmed a new border "face-off" between Indian and Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh, raising questions about the still fragile thaw in relations between New Delhi and…

image.caption: The de facto border between India and China runs through a remote mountainous areaImage: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Indo-Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) Director General Shatrujeet Kapur sounded alarm bells across India by confirming that Indian and Chinese troops had confronted each other at several locations along the de facto border in Arunachal Pradesh state, in India's northeast.
"In the past few days, a situation arose where a face-off happened (with Chinese troops) at various locations in Arunachal and it still continues," he told reporters last month.
"It may be difficult to counter China by conventional means because their PLA and BDR (Border Defense Regiment) have gone way ahead with investment and modernization," he said.
The disputed China-India border runs through a remote mountainous region.
Throughout the decades, clashes along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto border, have repeatedly triggered security crises between the world's two most populous nations.
Ties between Beijing and New Delhi are still affected by the deadly violence in 2020, when both countries accused each other of trying to seize territory.

In June that year, a clash in the Galwan River valley in eastern Ladakh killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops, according to Indian sources. China later confirmed four of its soldiers died.
Arunachal Pradesh leader Pema Khandu says situation normal

Kapur's remarks have brought renewed attention to the Himalayan frontier. Arunachal Pradesh Chief Minister Pema Khandu has acknowledged but also downplayed the border transgressions, saying such incidents were not new and the situation along the border was normal.
Khandu acknowledged that the border was not properly demarcated and that China did not recognize the McMahon Line, drawn by the British Empire in 1914, which separates Arunachal Pradesh from Tibet.
It was also not clear if the latest confrontations between the Chinese and Indian troops involved physical violence.
Tracking the tense relationship between India and China
China rejects wrongdoing

The opposition Congress party criticized Khandu's remarks, and accused the ruling BJP, led by India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi, of "rationalizing" Chinese actions instead of asserting India's position.

"On this there has been a deafening silence from the PM and his establishment," Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said in a post on X, referring to the face-offs confirmed by the border police chief.
Meanwhile, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal attributed the incidents to Chinese forces changing up their patrol routes.
"As we have noted in the past, the situation in the India-China border areas gets disturbed from time to time when Chinese forces diverge from established patrolling patterns," he said.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun rejected the allegations, saying Chinese troops were conducting "normal patrols" and strictly abiding by bilateral agreements.
Why do face-offs keep happening?
The LAC largely separates Indian- and Chinese-controlled territory. However, as forces from both nations patrol territory they regard as their own, they sometimes venture into disputed areas.
"There is a very simple reason — because there is no agreed line between the two," Gautam Bambawale, a former Indian ambassador to China, told DW.

The de-facto border stretches for 3,488 kilometres (2,167 miles) according to India, but China claims it is shorter. The two countries have held 25 rounds of talks between their Special Representatives since 2003, but have yet to reach a boundary settlement.
The dispute is particularly sensitive in Arunachal Pradesh, which China claims as part of southern Tibet.
Finding home in exile: Tibetans in India resist China
China building a hydropower dam in Tibet
Aravind Yelery, a China expert at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said the region has become more strategically important to Beijing.
"Both sides patrol a contested LAC, so friction is built into the arrangement," Yelery told DW.

"What is new is China's intensified focus on the eastern sector. Since announcing the 60,000-megawatt Medog hydropower project in Tibet, Beijing has poured infrastructure, troops, engineers and machinery into the area."
South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere

He described the LAC as "not a thin line but a deep zone of overlapping claims where patrols inevitably meet." Face-offs will continue, he argued, until diplomacy produces concrete arrangements on the ground.
According to Yelery, the diplomatic pledges made by Indian and Chinese leaders will take time to implement.
"A wide gap separates the leaders' promises from the measures that would prevent a repeat of 2020, namely disengagement and mutual restraint," he added.
What is different about the latest developments?
For India, the immediate concern is whether the recent encounters reflect familiar patrol disputes or a more significant change in Chinese activity along the frontier.
Ashok Kantha, another former Indian ambassador to China, said Chinese transgressions in the eastern sector were not new, but that their location and extent mattered.
"If the Chinese have now made deeper intrusions on our side of the LAC, or established a presence in new areas, or expanded their existing presence, that would be a serious development," he added.
He also pointed to agreements signed by the two countries to maintain peace along the border.

"Any such transgression would be in complete violation of several border-related agreements India and China have signed (1993, 1996, 2005, 2012 and 2013). In these, both sides committed to respect and strictly observe the LAC, and not to alter the status quo."
The Indian government has not publicly provided details of the locations or circumstances of the latest face-offs, making it unclear whether they have changed the situation on the ground.
A fragile diplomatic thaw

The renewed encounters come as India and China try to stabilize relations and move past the 2020 clashes. Both Beijing and New Delhi made reconciliatory moves, including restoring some direct flights and easing restrictions on travel and economic exchanges.

The diplomatic reset gathered pace after Narendra Modi and Xi Jinping met at the BRICS summit in Kazan, Russia, in October 2024. They met again at the SCO summit in Tianjin in August 2025 and at the BRICS summit in New Delhi this year.
The boundary dispute, however, remains unresolved.
India builds tunnel in Himalayas to counter China threat
Alka Acharya, director of the Institute of Chinese Studies in New Delhi, cautioned against drawing conclusions about the latest encounters without more information.
The government has described the incidents as face-offs, she said, but has not indicated that Chinese troops have taken control of Indian territory.

"The question is what is the nature of the so-called 'clashes' … not why the clashes are happening again? Any opinion on this latest kerfuffle would at best be conjecture without any definitive evidence," Acharya told DW.

Border incidents have occurred regularly over the past decade and a half, despite political and diplomatic negotiations. The unresolved dispute, she added, will continue to sustain distrust and constrain the broader relationship.
Whether the latest encounters signal a more serious escalation will depend on details that New Delhi has yet to make public.

articles.title: How Berlin's Arab queers are building their community
articles.summary: As the co-founder of the ADIRA Drag Festival, Lebanese performance artist, drag performer, DJ and cultural organizer Hassandra has become an essential part of Berlin's queer artistic landscape.

image.caption: Hassandra performing at the ADIRA Drag FestivalImage: Gönna Ketels/DW

blocks.text: "Adira" is an Arabic slang term used in Levantine queer culture to describe someone with a strong presence — someone powerful and accomplished.

It is also the name of a Berlin-based collective that curates events and club nights celebrating the diversity of queer Arab* culture. The asterisk signals the inclusion of non-Arab ethnic minorities and people with diverse identities and roots in Southwest Asia and North Africa.
Among the collective's events is the ADIRA Drag Festival, which celebrated its third edition in Berlin in late October.

This year's theme, "Who's Your Diva?!," brought together drag performers paying tribute to legendary figures from across the Eastern Mediterranean who have become queer icons — from Egyptian music legend Umm Kulthum to Turkish star Bülent Ersoy and Lebanese pop icon Haifa Wehbe.
Hassandra, co-founder of ADIRA and the ADIRA Drag Festival, was among the performers, taking on the persona of Lebanese pop star Elissa.
Inspired by 'imperfect' divas

"It is very important for me to bring my Lebanese Arab identity and culture into what I do, because I think it's a very beautiful culture. And there's a lot of campy, glamorous, beautiful divas," Hassandra said.

Elissa's "whole discography is very romantic, raw, soft, kind of like very Adele vibes," Hassandra told DW ahead of the October 30 show. "However, her personality is known to be the extreme opposite. She's very feisty. Very blunt, very unfiltered. Not soft at all as a person." The star is also known for speaking out on political issues in Lebanon. She has publicly voiced support for LGBTQ+ communities in the Middle East, while also frequently sparking controversy across the Arab world with her outspoken positions on other political issues.
Hassandra's ADIRA Drag Festival performance addresses this complexity, ultimately "tapping into her sort of controversial political opinions," the drag artist explained.

This reflects one of the ideas Hassandra hopes to promote with the theme of this year's festival. "As queer people, we tend to idealize a lot of pop divas. But these pop divas are very imperfect in their nature," Hassandra said. The show provides an opportunity to critically revisit these divas' legacy through a more critical lens. "And this sort of critical lens can be taken into the outside world, as in: never follow anyone in life blindly. No one should follow any politician, any political party, any pop diva, any activist blindly."

blocks.caption: Hassandra out of drag: They are also a DJ and cultural organizerImage: Gönna Ketels/DW

blocks.text: Building community through drag

Born in Beirut in 1994, Hassandra studied theater and stage acting at the Lebanese University before moving to Berlin in 2017. "I would say it was it was just a very sort of impulsive decision at the age of 22. I mean, there's no doubt that the economic situation was really bad in Lebanon and continued to become even worse," the artist said.
In Berlin, Hassandra became increasingly involved in the city's independent art scene and queer nightlife. Drag emerged as another form of self-expression for the actor.
Through performances that combine theatrical intensity, political humor, grotesque aesthetics and moments of tenderness, Hassandra challenges conventional understandings of gender and identity.

Their work explores themes of home, nostalgia, displacement and queer Arab culture. These ideas are also central to ADIRA, which Hassandra founded in 2023 with Syrian-German DJ and cultural producer Zuher Jazmati, also known as xanax_attax.
Through panel discussions, performances and music events, ADIRA fosters collective participation and community-building.
As Islamophobia and homophobia rise alongside the far right, spaces like ADIRA offer a sense of belonging and support for Arab queer communities.
That sense of community has become even more important following the deadly Islamist terrorist attack during Berlin's Christopher Street Day pride parade in July.
What does the Berlin Pride attack mean for city's identity?
In the aftermath, Hassandra felt caught between their different identities. As an Arab queer person, "you fall in this position where then you start receiving a lot of racism," they said.

"And I think this is why it's important, for us queer Arabs, to say we are sad over what happened, but that we also reject any of the racism that comes from that," Hassandra said. "I think we [the Arab community] are being used in a lot of ways as a punching bag for a lot of things that are happening."
Rather than allowing the attack to fuel hatred and racism, Hassandra said, "we should make Germany a safer place for everyone to live in."
"There's place for everyone. It's a huge country," they added.
The interview with Hassandra was conducted by Gönna Ketels.

articles.title: Cyprus: From ties with Russia to a strategic alignment with the US
articles.summary: The Republic of Cyprus long balanced ties between Russia and the West. Now, it is phasing out Russian weapons, expanding defense cooperation with the United States and redefining its place in the…

image.caption: US Ambassador to Cyprus John Breslow said in October that 'the United States will protect Cyprus in the future'Image: Brandon Williams-Church/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: In an interview with the Cyprus News Agency on October 4, the new US ambassador to Cyprus, John Breslow, outlined plans to upgrade the Andreas Papandreou Air Base in Paphos to accommodate large US military transport aircraft.
He also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports and an expansion of joint military activities.
But one statement carried particular political weight: his assurance that "the United States will protect Cyprus in the future."
Although the remark does not constitute a formal US security guarantee, it reflects the growing cooperation between the two countries.

For a country that for decades maintained close ties with Moscow, viewed US foreign policy with suspicion and is not a member of NATO, the prospect of an expanded American military presence marks a significant geopolitical shift.

blocks.caption: The ambassador also announced plans for more frequent visits by US warships to Cypriot ports. Pictured here: US amphibious assault ship USS Wasp docked at the port in Limassol in 2024Image: Iakovos Hatzistavrou/AFP

blocks.text: It is perhaps the clearest indication yet of Cyprus's gradual loosening of ties with Russia and its increasingly close strategic alignment with the United States.
The nonalignment years
The shift is particularly striking given Cyprus's political history.
In the years after it gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1960, the Republic of Cyprus sought to balance its relations between East and West.

Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III, the first president of independent Cyprus, the country became a founding member in 1961 of the Non-Aligned Movement, a forum of nations that did not align with either of the two superpowers of the day: the United States and the Soviet Union.

blocks.caption: Under the leadership of Archbishop Makarios III (left), Cyprus became a founding member of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961Image: Nicholas Tsikourias/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: This approach allowed Nicosia to maintain close ties with the Soviet Union without severing its connections to the West.
EU membership
Even after joining the European Union in 2004, Cyprus maintained strong political, economic and military ties with Moscow.
Relations with the United States, by contrast, remained overshadowed by the Turkish invasion of the island in 1974 and the US's failure to take decisive action against Ankara.
The United States prioritized maintaining its strategic relationship with Turkey, a key NATO ally, over taking a tougher stance against the invasion.

The US position fueled widespread anti-American sentiment in Cyprus, culminating in a violent demonstration outside the embassy in Nicosia on August 19, 1974, during which US Ambassador Roger Davies was shot dead.

Mistrust deepened further in 1987, when the United States imposed an arms embargo on the Republic of Cyprus, officially intended to prevent an arms race on the island and avoid undermining efforts to resolve the Cyprus conflict.
Close relations with Moscow

The US arms embargo contributed to the reliance of the Cypriot National Guard (the armed forces of the Republic of Cyprus) on Russia-made weapons systems, strengthening the Kremlin's position as a major military partner.
The response by Cyprus to Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014 illustrated the strength of these ties.

The Cypriot government expressed serious reservations about imposing tougher EU sanctions on Russia. Then-Foreign Minister Ioannis Kasoulides warned that such measures could have devastating consequences for the Cypriot economy.

blocks.caption: Even after joining the EU in 2004, Cyprus maintained close ties with Moscow. Pictured here: Nicos Anastasiades (left), president of the Republic of Cyprus, and Russian President Vladimir Putin after signing agreements in Russia in 2015Image: Nikita Shvetsov/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Relations with Moscow deepened further in February 2015, when President Nicos Anastasiades visited the Russian capital and signed a series of agreements with President Vladimir Putin.

These included a naval cooperation memorandum facilitating visits by Russian warships to Cypriot ports. Moscow also agreed to more favorable repayment terms for its €2.5 billion loan to Cyprus in 2011.

Cooperation remained close as recently as October 2021, when then Foreign Minister and current President Nikos Christodoulides signed a Strategic Cooperation Framework for 2022–2024 in Moscow alongside his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov.
Turning point in 2022
The decisive turning point came just four months later, in February 2022, with Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Konstantinos Adamides, an associate professor of international relations at the University of Nicosia, told DW that the invasion accelerated a geopolitical shift toward the West that had already begun.
"For the first time, the Republic of Cyprus openly and unequivocally chose to side with the West, despite the economic and political costs of breaking with Moscow," Adamides said.
Nicosia aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia, despite the Cypriot economy's strong links to Moscow, particularly in services, investment and tourism.
The decision marked a significant departure from Cyprus's traditional foreign policy approach of maintaining a balance between Russia and the West.
Adamides said the government's position on Russia paved the way for closer relations with the United States, particularly in the field of security.

blocks.caption: Cyprus is seeking to gradually reduce its dependence on Russian military equipment. Pictured here: Russian-made T-80 tanks in a 2021 military parade in Nicosia Image: Philippos Christou/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cyprus, he said, succeeded in convincing Washington that it could serve as a reliable partner in the Eastern Mediterranean.
What form does the rapprochement take?
The rapprochement had already gained an institutional foundation before the war, with a bilateral statement of intent on security cooperation signed in 2018.

Further initiatives followed, including the Cyprus Center for Land, Open-seas and Port Security (CYCLOPS), a US-funded training facility inaugurated in Larnaca in April 2022. The center provides training for security personnel from Cyprus and other countries in the region in areas such as port security, counterterrorism and preventing the trafficking of hazardous materials.
An even more significant development for the Cypriot National Guard came in September 2022, when Washington announced the full suspension of the arms embargo imposed in 1987.

The decision allowed for the export of lethal military equipment to Cyprus, subject to the necessary US approvals. The suspension, which was not permanent and remains subject to periodic renewal, has been renewed until September 30, 2027.
Cyprus and NATO
The strategic security reorientation is also significant because Cyprus is not a member of NATO.
The crash landing of an Iranian done on the British military base at Akrotiri in March reignited a debate in Cyprus about whether the country should join NATO.

blocks.caption: Earlier this year President Nikos Christodoulides said that Cyprus would apply to join NATO 'even tomorrow if it were possible'Image: Nicolas Tucat/AFP

blocks.text: At the time, Christodoulides said Cyprus was preparing for potential membership at the military, operational and administrative level and would apply to join NATO "even tomorrow if it were possible."
Christodoulides said, however, that joining the alliance was not possible because "the political conditions are not there, taking into account the well-known position of Turkey."
Phasing out Russian weapons
The country's changing strategic orientation is also reflected in the modernization of its armed forces.
